# ArkType

> TypeScript's 1:1 validator

# Setup

> Install ArkType and configure TypeScript to infer your types correctly.

## Installation

```bash
npm install arktype
```

```ts
import { type } from "arktype"

const User = type({
	name: "string",
	"age?": "number.integer >= 0"
})

// ArkErrors: age must be non-negative (was -1)
const out = User({ name: "Alan", age: -1 })
```

## Requirements

- TypeScript `>=5.1`, including TypeScript 7.
- An ESM project. ArkType is ESM-only, but a CommonJS project can `require` it on runtimes that support `require(esm)`, like Node `>=20.19` or `>=22.12`.

```json
{
	"compilerOptions": {
		"strict": true,
		"skipLibCheck": true,
		"exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true
	}
}
```

- [`strict`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig#strict), or at least [`strictNullChecks`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig#strictNullChecks), is required for inference to work.
- [`skipLibCheck`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig#skipLibCheck) is recommended. It avoids harmless errors from differences between your config and ours (see [FAQ](https://arktype.io/docs/faq#why-do-i-see-type-errors-in-an-arktype-package-in-node_modules)) and speeds up your editor.
- [`exactOptionalPropertyTypes`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig#exactOptionalPropertyTypes) is recommended. It makes your inferred types match runtime behavior. ArkType rejects `undefined` for an optional key unless its value allows it, so without this flag, `typeof User.infer` accepts `{ age: undefined }` while `User` rejects it.

ArkType runs in Node, Deno, Bun, browsers and edge runtimes. Under a strict Content-Security-Policy, enable [`jitless`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#jitless) so it never tries `new Function`, or [precompile](#precompile) your Types.

## Precompile

If your app is bundled, add [`@ark/precompile`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile) to your bundler. Every Type you define is then compiled when you build into a standalone validator, so arktype's parser never ships and nothing is compiled at runtime:

```bash
npm install -D @ark/precompile
```

```ts
import { precompile } from "@ark/precompile/unplugin"
import { defineConfig } from "vite"

export default defineConfig({
	plugins: [precompile.vite()]
})
```

Your definitions don't change, and you can add it at any time. [Setup](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup) covers the other bundlers, test runners and Next.

## Next

If you configure ArkType globally, your config has to load before anything imports `arktype`. See [Configuration](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration).

The other packages ArkType publishes, and what to import from each entrypoint, are listed in [Packages](https://arktype.io/docs/packages). If you're upgrading an existing project, [Upgrading](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading) lists the changes that can break your code.

Next, set up [your editor](https://arktype.io/docs/editor) or start with [your first type](https://arktype.io/docs/intro/your-first-type).

# Your first type

> Define a type with TypeScript syntax, compose it, and validate data with it.

If you already know TypeScript, you already know most of ArkType's syntax.

## Define

```ts
import { type } from "arktype"

const User = type({
	name: "string",
	platform: "'android' | 'ios'",
	"versions?": "(number | string)[]"
})

// { name: string; platform: "android" | "ios"; versions?: (number | string)[] }
type User = typeof User.infer
```

A key ending in `?` is optional, as in TypeScript. String literals like `'android'` need their own quotes inside the definition.

Definitions are checked by TypeScript, so a mistake is an error in your editor, with autocomplete to help fix it:

```ts
const User = type({
	name: "strng"
	// TypeScript: 'strng' is unresolvable
})
```

## Compose

Suppose we want to move `platform` and `versions` from our original type to a new `device` property.

```ts
const User = type({
	name: "string",
	// nested definitions don't need to be wrapped
	device: {
		platform: "'android' | 'ios'",
		"versions?": "(number | string)[]"
	}
})
```

To decouple `device` from `User`, move it to its own type and reference it.

```ts
const Device = type({
	platform: "'android' | 'ios'",
	"versions?": "(number | string)[]"
})

const User = type({
	name: "string",
	device: Device
})
```

## Validate

Call a type with `unknown` data to get back either the validated data or an `ArkErrors` object describing every problem.

```ts
const out = User({
	name: "Alan Turing",
	device: {
		platform: "enigma",
		versions: [0, "1", 0n]
	}
})

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	// ArkErrors: device.platform must be "android" or "ios" (was "enigma")
	//            device.versions[2] must be a number or a string (was a bigint)
	console.error(out.summary)
} else {
	// out is narrowed to the validated User
	console.log(`Hello, ${out.name}`)
}
```

Calling a type never throws for invalid data. Each problem is in `out.issues`, with its `path`, `code` and `message`; see [Errors](https://arktype.io/docs/errors).

Where invalid data is a bug rather than something to handle, use `.assert`. It returns the validated data or throws a `TraversalError` describing the same problems.

```ts
// TraversalError: name must be a string (was missing)
const user = User.assert({})
```

You now know how to define a `Type` and use it to check your data at runtime.

Next, we'll look at how ArkType extends TypeScript's type system with runtime constraints like `string.email` or `number.integer < 100`.

# Adding constraints

> Narrow types beyond what TypeScript can express, with keywords, ranges, divisors and custom predicates.

TypeScript can represent types like `string` or `number`, but what about `email` or `integer less than 100`?

In ArkType, conditions that narrow a type beyond its **basis** are called **constraints**. They compose with TypeScript's operators like any other part of a definition.

## Define

Let's create a new `Contact` Type that enforces our example constraints.

```ts
const Contact = type({
	// many common constraints are available as built-in keywords
	email: "string.email",
	// others can be written as type-safe expressions
	score: "number.integer < 100"
})

// infer the TypeScript type as usual
type Contact = typeof Contact.infer
```

> **number excludes NaN and Infinity**
>
> `number` rejects `NaN`, `Infinity` and `-Infinity` by default. To allow them,
> see `number.NaN`, `number.Infinity` and `number.NegativeInfinity` in
> [Keywords](https://arktype.io/docs/keywords), or the `numberAllowsNaN` and
> `numberAllowsInfinity` options in [Configuration](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration).

## Compose

Imagine we want to define a new Type representing a non-empty list of `Contact`.

Definitions create new types. Chained methods refine or transform types you already have.

```ts
// a non-empty list of Contact
const Contacts = Contact.array().atLeastLength(1)

// ArkErrors: must be non-empty
const out = Contacts([])
```

## Narrow

Structured constraints like divisors and ranges will only take us so far. For anything else, add your own logic with `.narrow`.

```ts
// there's no "not divisible" expression - need to narrow
const Odd = type("number").narrow((n, ctx) =>
	// if even, add a customizable error and return false
	n % 2 === 0 ? ctx.mustBe("odd") : true
)

const FavoriteNumbers = type({
	even: "number % 2",
	odd: Odd
})

const out = FavoriteNumbers({
	even: 7,
	odd: 8
})

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	// ArkErrors: even must be even (was 7)
	//            odd must be odd (was 8)
	console.error(out.summary)
} else {
	console.log(out.odd)
}
```

You now know how to refine your types to enforce additional constraints at runtime.

But what if once your input is fully validated, you still need to make some adjustments before it's ready to use?

The final section of the intro covers **morphs**, which transform data as part of a Type.

# Morphs

> Transform data as part of validation by piping it through functions and other Types.

Sometimes, data at the boundaries of your code needs more than validation before it's ready to use.

**Morphs** transform your data. You can **pipe** them before, after or between validators, and chain them to other morphs.

```ts
// Type<(In: string) => Out<object>>
const parseJson = type("string").pipe((s): object => JSON.parse(s))

// { ark: "type" }
const out = parseJson('{ "ark": "type" }')

// ArkErrors: must be a string (was an object)
const badOut = parseJson(out)
```

This is a good start, but what happens if we pass a string that isn't valid JSON?

```ts
// Uncaught SyntaxError: Expected property name ☠️
const badOut = parseJson('{ unquoted: "keys" }')
```

By default, ArkType assumes that if one of your morphs or narrows throws, you intend to crash. For a function you don't trust, use `pipe.try`, which turns what it throws into an error:

```ts
const parseJson = type("string").pipe.try((s): object => JSON.parse(s))

const out = parseJson('{ unquoted: "keys" }')

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	// ArkErrors: must be valid according to an anonymous predicate (was aborted due to error:
	//                SyntaxError: Expected property name or '}' in JSON at position 2 (line 1 column 3)
	//            )
	console.error(out.summary)
}
```

A validated `object` still isn't very useful, though. Since a Type can be called like a function, it can be a step in a pipe too. For JSON, the built-in `string.json.parse` keyword does the parsing, and `.to` validates its output:

```ts
// .to is a sugared .pipe for a single parsed output validator
const parseJson = type("string.json.parse").to({
	name: "string",
	version: "string.semver"
})

const out = parseJson('{ "name": true, "version": "v2.0.0" }')

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	// ArkErrors: name must be a string (was boolean)
	//            version must be a semantic version (see https://semver.org/) (was "v2.0.0")
	console.error(out.summary)
} else {
	// { name: string; version: string }
	console.log(`${out.name}:${out.version}`)
}
```

> **Morphs receive your data, not a copy**
>
> A morph is passed the validated value itself. If it mutates its argument, it
> mutates the caller's data, so return a new value instead.

```ts
const addTag = type({ tags: "string[]" }).pipe(o => ({
	...o,
	tags: [...o.tags, "new"]
}))
```

When you're ready to ship, [precompile](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile) your Types: the same definitions, compiled when you build into standalone validators that carry only the checks they need.

You now have the fundamentals you need to bring your types to runtime. The rest of the docs cover each part of the API in depth, starting with [primitives](https://arktype.io/docs/primitives).

# Cheat sheet

> ArkType's most common syntax, patterns and gotchas on one page.

A quick reference for ArkType's most common patterns. The [skill for agents](https://arktype.io/docs/agents) covers the same ground.

## Syntax kinds

ArkType offers several ways to define the same type. Use whichever fits your context.

```ts
import { type } from "arktype"

// string expression — most concise
const StringSyntax = type("string | number")

// tuple expression — embed non-string operands
const TupleSyntax = type(["string", "|", "number"])

// chained — compose existing types
const Chained = type("string").or("number")
```

## Keywords

Keywords follow a `typescriptType.constraint.subconstraint` pattern. See [Keywords](https://arktype.io/docs/keywords) for the full list.

```ts
// string keywords
type("string.email") // email address
type("string.uuid") // UUID
type("string.url") // parsable URL
type("string.trim") // morph: trims whitespace
type("string.json.parse") // morph: string → parsed JSON
type("string.date.parse") // morph: string → Date

// number keywords
type("number.integer") // whole numbers
type("number.safe") // between MIN_SAFE_INTEGER and MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, not necessarily an integer
type("number.epoch") // integer ms timestamp a Date can hold
```

`number` rejects `NaN`, `Infinity` and `-Infinity`. Add `number.NaN`, `number.Infinity` or `number.NegativeInfinity` to allow them.

## Operators

```ts
type("string | number") // union
type("string.email & /@arktype\\.io$/") // intersection
type("number > 0") // exclusive min
type("number >= 0") // inclusive min
type("string <= 255") // max length
type("number % 2") // divisible by 2
```

## Objects

```ts
const User = type({
	name: "string",
	"email?": "string.email", // optional key — use '?' suffix in the key
	age: "number >= 0 = 0" // default value — implicitly optional
})

// index signatures (Record types)
const Env = type({
	"[string]": "string" // Record<string, string>
})

// undeclared keys are allowed by default; reject or remove them
const Strict = type({ "+": "reject", name: "string" })
const Stripped = type({ "+": "delete", name: "string" })
```

## Arrays and tuples

```ts
const Strings = type("string[]") // string expression
const Numbers = type.number.array() // chained

// tuples — fixed length and positional types
const Pair = type(["string", "number"])

// GOTCHA: type([X]) is a 1-element tuple, NOT an array
const Item = type({ id: "string" })
const Wrong = type([Item]) // tuple of exactly [Item]
const Right = Item.array() // Item[]

// readonly
const Ids = type("string[]").readonly() // readonly string[]
```

## Enumerations

```ts
const Role = type("'admin' | 'member'") // literals need their own quotes
const Size = type.enumerated(1, 2, 3)

enum Color {
	Red = "red",
	Blue = "blue"
}
const ColorValue = type.valueOf(Color)
```

## Composition

```ts
const Device = type({
	platform: "'android' | 'ios'",
	"version?": "string"
})

// reference in another type by passing it directly
const User = type({
	name: "string",
	device: Device
})

// fluent composition
const Admin = User.and({ role: "'admin'" })
const Guest = type({ name: "string" }).or({ token: "string" })
const Draft = User.partial()
const Name = User.pick("name")
```

## Recursive types

```ts
import { scope } from "arktype"

const types = scope({
	TreeNode: {
		value: "number",
		children: "TreeNode[]"
	}
}).export()

const tree = types.TreeNode({ value: 1, children: [] })
```

## Morphs and pipes

```ts
// .to() — parse, then validate the output
const parsePort = type("string.integer.parse").to("0 < number <= 65535")

// .pipe() — validated input → transform function
const toUpper = type("string").pipe(s => s.toUpperCase())

// built-in parse morphs
const parseDate = type("string.date.parse") // string → Date
const parseJson = type("string.json.parse") // string → parsed JSON
const trim = type("string.trim") // string → trimmed string
```

## Custom rules

```ts
const Signup = type({
	password: "string >= 8",
	confirmPassword: "string"
}).narrow(
	(data, ctx) =>
		data.password === data.confirmPassword ||
		ctx.reject({
			expected: "identical to password",
			actual: "",
			path: ["confirmPassword"]
		})
)
```

## Matching

```ts
import { match } from "arktype"

const sizeOf = match({
	string: s => s.length,
	number: n => n,
	default: "assert"
})

sizeOf("abc") // 3
```

## Type inference

```ts
const User = type({
	name: "string",
	"age?": "number"
})

// extract the TypeScript type
type User = typeof User.infer
// { name: string; age?: number }
```

## Error handling

```ts
const User = type({
	name: "string",
	"age?": "number"
})

const out = User({ name: "Alan", age: "not a number" })

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	// ArkErrors: age must be a number (was a string)
	console.error(out.summary)
	// plain objects, each with its path, code and message
	out.issues[0].path
} else {
	// out is typed as { name: string; age?: number }
	console.log(out.name)
}

// returns the validated data or throws
const user = User.assert({ name: "Alan" })
```

## Interop

```ts
// a Standard Schema, accepted by tRPC, Hono, oRPC, the MCP SDK and others
User["~standard"]

// { $schema: "...", type: "object", properties: { ... }, required: ["name"] }
User.toJsonSchema()
```

Global configuration goes through `configure` from `arktype/config`, in a file that runs before anything imports `arktype`. See [Configuration](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration).

## Precompile

```ts
// vite.config.ts: every Type becomes a standalone validator at build time
export default {
	plugins: [precompile.vite()]
}
```

## Common gotchas

| Mistake | Fix |
| - | - |
| `name: "string \| undefined"` for optional | Use `"name?": "string"` — append `?` to the **key** |
| `type([Schema])` for arrays | Use `Schema.array()` — brackets create tuples |
| ``type(`${Schema}[]`)`` | Use `Schema.array()` or `[Schema, "[]"]` — never interpolate a Type |
| `"Record<string, T>"` with `T` a variable | Use `type.Record("string", T)` or `{ "[string]": T }` |
| `type("number = 0")` | Defaults only work as object values or tuple elements |
| `out[0]` or `out.map(...)` on errors | Use `out.issues[0]` or `out.issues.map(...)` |
| Mutating the argument in `.pipe` | Return a new value; a morph receives the caller's data, not a copy |
| `type User = typeof Schema.t` | Use `typeof Schema.infer` for the output type |
| Precompiled: `User.and(...)` called at runtime | Compose inside a definition: `const Admin = User.and(...)` |
| Precompiled: `type()` from a runtime value | Make it static, mark it `// @ark-runtime`, or build with `runtime: "arktype"` |

# Agents

> Help Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and other coding agents write ArkType.

## Skill

The ArkType [skill](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/blob/main/ark/type/skills/arktype/SKILL.md) tells agents when to reach for ArkType, how its syntax maps to TypeScript, and which mistakes to avoid. Add it to your project with:

```bash
npx skills add arktypeio/arktype
```

This installs the skill from the repository's default branch, which tracks the latest release. The `arktype` package also includes the skill at `skills/arktype/SKILL.md`, so tools like [skills-npm](https://github.com/antfu/skills-npm) can link the copy that matches your installed version.

## Docs as Markdown

Every page of these docs is available as Markdown by adding `.md` to its URL, e.g. [/docs/intro/setup.md](https://arktype.io/docs/intro/setup.md). The buttons under each page's title copy it or open it in Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor.

[/llms.txt](https://arktype.io/llms.txt) is an index of every page, with a link to its Markdown and a one-line description, following the [llms.txt](https://llmstxt.org) convention. [/llms-full.txt](https://arktype.io/llms-full.txt) has the full text of every ArkType page in one file. Attest's docs are at [/docs/attest/llms.txt](https://arktype.io/docs/attest/llms.txt) and ArkRegex's at [/docs/regex/llms.txt](https://arktype.io/docs/regex/llms.txt).

## Precompile

When an agent runs your local dev, a build step costs it a loop it's good at: build, read the error, fix, rebuild. So [precompiling](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile) costs little, and it ships every Type as a standalone validator.

Each problem the build reports names the file, line and column, what it couldn't do, why, and how to fix it:

```
src/forms.ts:14:19  type(`string <= ${limit}`) cannot be precompiled
  `limit` is a parameter of makeField (src/forms.ts:12:22); its value is known only at runtime
  Standalone builds construct every Type at build time. Make it static, or build with runtime: "arktype".
```

`npx arktype-precompile --check "src/**/*.ts"` lists every such problem at once without bundling, and [shadow mode](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#shadow-mode) fails a test wherever a precompiled validator would behave otherwise than arktype. [Troubleshooting](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/troubleshooting) lists the fix for each report.

## AGENTS.md

If your project has an `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md`, a line like this keeps agents on ArkType when they add validation:

```
Validate untrusted input with ArkType. Docs: https://arktype.io/llms.txt
```

If you precompile, add:

```
ArkType definitions are precompiled when the app builds. Fix each precompile error as its hint says; don't set allowUnsafe to get past one.
```

## Building agents

ArkType types are [Standard Schemas](https://arktype.io/docs/standard-schema) that can also produce JSON Schema, so libraries that need both accept them directly. For example, the [MCP TypeScript SDK](https://ts.sdk.modelcontextprotocol.io/v2/advanced/schema-libraries) (`@modelcontextprotocol/server`) takes an ArkType type as a tool's `inputSchema` as-is. It derives the JSON Schema the model sees from it, and validates the model's arguments before your handler runs:

```ts
// server is an McpServer from @modelcontextprotocol/server
server.registerTool(
	"greet",
	{
		description: "Greet someone by name",
		inputSchema: type({ name: "string", "times?": "1 <= number.integer <= 5" })
	},
	async ({ name, times }) => ({
		content: [{ type: "text", text: `Hello, ${name}! `.repeat(times ?? 1) }]
	})
)
```

Calling `greet` with `times: 99` returns an error result to the model with ArkType's message, `times must be at most 5 (was 99)`, so it knows what to fix.

# Editor setup

> Highlighting, inline errors and autocomplete for ArkType definitions in VS Code, JetBrains IDEs and other editors.

ArkType works in any editor with TypeScript support. These extensions make definitions read like the rest of your code.

## VS Code

Install [ArkType](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=arktypeio.arkdark) (`arktypeio.arkdark`). It's also on [Open VSX](https://open-vsx.org/extension/arktypeio/arkdark) for Cursor, VSCodium and Windsurf. It adds:

- syntax highlighting for strings in ArkType definitions, in `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.js`, `.jsx`, `.mdx`, `.svelte`, `.vue`, `.astro` and Markdown files
- one-line summaries of ArkType's type errors at the end of the line, through [ErrorLens](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=usernamehw.errorlens), which it installs as a dependency
- the setting `"editor.quickSuggestions": { "strings": "on" }`, so you get completions while typing an expression like `"string | num"`

It also sets ErrorLens to show the message of the problem closest to your cursor, with no delay and without the hover buttons, and to show only the part of an ArkType error that names the fix, like `"number | string"` for `"number | strin"`. Each is an ordinary default, so a value in your own settings for `errorLens.followCursor`, `errorLens.delay`, `errorLens.editorHoverPartsEnabled` or `errorLens.replace` overrides it.

To have auto-import pick ArkType's `type` instead of the `type` function from Node's `os` module, add this to `.vscode/settings.json`:

```json
{
	"typescript.preferences.autoImportSpecifierExcludeRegexes": ["^(node:)?os$"]
}
```

### Themes

[ArkThemes](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=arktypeio.arkthemes) (`arktypeio.arkthemes`, also on [Open VSX](https://open-vsx.org/extension/arktypeio/arkthemes)) is a separate extension with **ArkDark**, which these docs use for code, and **ArkLight**, each with an italic variant. They highlight TypeScript generics distinctly. You don't need them for the ArkType extension to work.

## JetBrains IDEs

The [ArkType plugin](https://plugins.jetbrains.com/plugin/27099-arktype), maintained by Jan-Niklas Wortmann, adds syntax highlighting for ArkType definitions to WebStorm, IntelliJ IDEA and other JetBrains IDEs.

## Other editors

There's no official extension for other editors yet. For Neovim, a community [tree-sitter grammar](https://github.com/jeffrom/tree-sitter-arktype) covers the most common syntax. If you'd like to help add support for another editor, see [this issue](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/issues/989).

Completions and type errors come from TypeScript, so they work in every editor without an extension.

# Precompile

> Compile your Types when you build, and ship only the checks they need

ArkType runs in two modes. Both take the same definitions and infer the same types.

- **Dynamic**: `type()` parses each definition at runtime and compiles it the first time your program uses it. No build step.
- **Precompiled**: [`@ark/precompile`](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/tree/main/ark/precompile) constructs your Types when you build. Each becomes a standalone validator that imports only `arktype/runtime`, so arktype's parser never ships and no code is generated at runtime.

```ts
import { precompile } from "@ark/precompile/unplugin"

export default {
	plugins: [precompile.vite()]
}
```

Your definitions stay as you wrote them. [Setup](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup) covers every bundler, test runner and Next.

## Speed and size

A validator that compiles at runtime ships its compiler, and one that interprets ships its interpreter. A precompiled build ships neither: only the checks your Types need, and the runtime that reports their errors. Pick the build: the fastest validator or the smallest, from the same definitions. The [options](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options) decide which: [`optimize: "size"`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#optimize) and dropping [`members`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#members) make a build smaller and its validators slower.

- Runtime (instructions per call, lower is better): moltar's parseSafe benchmark (validate, removing undeclared keys), instructions per call, Node 24. Source: moltar/typescript-runtime-type-benchmarks, https\://moltar.github.io/typescript-runtime-type-benchmarks/
- ArkType (precompiled): 189
- @ts-runtypes: 209
- Typia: 213
- ata-validator (AOT): 220
- ArkType (dynamic): 262

* Bundle size (B gzipped, lower is better): valibot.dev's login form, each reporting every error with a message; precompiled with its validator's members and methods, and its errors' methods, off. Source: valibot.dev's comparison, https\://valibot.dev/guides/comparison/
* ArkType (precompiled): 912
* Valibot: 1,475
* Zod Mini: 5,127
* Zod: 25,058
* ArkType (dynamic): 75,520

Precompiled ArkType is the fastest on moltar's parseSafe and assertLoose benchmarks, and on Valibot's own login form it reports every error, with its message, in a smaller bundle than Valibot. The charts come from different builds: each names its benchmark and the options it was built with.

Because every Type is built when you build, a precompiled validator has no initialization cost, and because nothing is generated at runtime, it runs under a Content-Security-Policy that blocks `eval`.

## Optimized by set theory

ArkType reduces every Type to a normalized set of constraints, so it knows which Types are subtypes of others, which overlap and which can't both be satisfied. Precompiling applies that knowledge in your build:

- **Unions discriminate themselves.** ArkType finds the key that tells a union's branches apart and switches on it, so data is checked against one branch rather than each in turn.
- **Redundant checks disappear.** `number > 0` intersected with `number >= 10` is `number >= 10`, one check, and a branch never rechecks the key it was chosen by.
- **Contradictions never ship.** A definition that intersects to nothing, like `{ id: string }` and `{ id: number }`, throws a ParseError, which fails the build rather than shipping a validator that rejects everything.

```ts
const Shape = type({
	kind: "'circle'",
	radius: "number > 0"
}).or({
	kind: "'square'",
	side: "number > 0"
})
```

Precompiled, `Shape` checks data like this, its helpers inlined:

```ts
data => {
	switch (data?.kind) {
		case "circle":
			return Number.isFinite(data.radius) && data.radius > 0
		case "square":
			return Number.isFinite(data.side) && data.side > 0
	}
	return false
}
```

## With agents

A build step costs a loop: build, read the error, fix, rebuild. When an agent runs your local dev, that loop is what it does best, so the cost of precompiling is small and its benefit is every validator you ship.

Precompiling stays quiet when everything builds. Where something would fail at runtime and the fix is clear, the build fails instead, with the file, line and column, what it couldn't do, why, and how to fix it:

```
src/forms.ts:14:19  type(`string <= ${limit}`) cannot be precompiled
  `limit` is a parameter of makeField (src/forms.ts:12:22); its value is known only at runtime
  Standalone builds construct every Type at build time. Make it static, or build with runtime: "arktype".
```

To make the loop shorter:

- Run [`arktype-precompile --check`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#check-an-existing-project) to list every definition the build would refuse, without bundling.
- Add the [ESLint rule](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#eslint) so the same errors show in the editor and in lint runs.
- Run tests in [shadow mode](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#shadow-mode), which fails a test wherever a precompiled validator would behave otherwise than arktype.
- Give your agent the [ArkType skill](https://arktype.io/docs/agents) so it writes definitions the build accepts on the first try.

## How a validator differs

A standalone validator validates, asserts and implements Standard Schema as the Type it replaces does. It doesn't compose or introspect: it lacks methods like `.and` and `.extends`, and its error messages say what failed without printing the value. The build fails wherever it sees your program rely on what a validator lacks. See [Validators](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/validators).

If you need the whole Type API at runtime, build with `runtime: "arktype"`: arktype ships, and each Type the build could precompile skips compiling at runtime. [Dynamic vs Precompiled](https://arktype.io/docs/dynamic-vs-precompiled) compares the three side by side.

# Setup

> Add precompilation to your bundler, test runner or framework

## Installation

```bash
npm install -D @ark/precompile
```

`@ark/precompile` runs on Node 22.12 or later, and precompiles with the version of `arktype` it imports, so install one copy of `arktype`. The build fails if your program resolves another version, or more than one copy of `arktype`, `@ark/schema` or `@ark/util`, naming each and the file that reached it. Each module of validators also imports an export of `arktype/runtime` named for its version, like `precompiledForArktype_2_2_9`, so a bundle or Node fails to link it to another version's runtime, e.g. one a stale cache kept. It adds nothing to the bundle.

## Bundlers

`@ark/precompile/unplugin` precompiles a program as your bundler builds it.

**Vite**

```ts
import { precompile } from "@ark/precompile/unplugin"
import { defineConfig } from "vite"

export default defineConfig({
	plugins: [precompile.vite()]
})
```

Vitest runs tests through the same plugin.

**Rollup**

```js
import { precompile } from "@ark/precompile/unplugin"
import { nodeResolve } from "@rollup/plugin-node-resolve"
import typescript from "@rollup/plugin-typescript"

export default {
	input: "src/main.ts",
	output: { file: "dist/main.js", format: "es" },
	plugins: [
		precompile.rollup(),
		nodeResolve({ extensions: [".ts", ".js"] }),
		typescript()
	]
}
```

Rolldown takes `precompile.rolldown()`.

**webpack**

```js
import { precompile } from "@ark/precompile/unplugin"

export default {
	entry: "./src/main.ts",
	resolve: { extensions: [".ts", ".js"] },
	module: {
		rules: [{ test: /\.ts$/, loader: "ts-loader" }]
	},
	plugins: [precompile.webpack()]
}
```

**Rspack**

```js
import { precompile } from "@ark/precompile/unplugin"

export default {
	entry: "./src/main.ts",
	resolve: { extensions: [".ts", ".js"] },
	module: {
		rules: [
			{
				test: /\.ts$/,
				loader: "builtin:swc-loader",
				options: { jsc: { parser: { syntax: "typescript" } } },
				type: "javascript/auto"
			}
		]
	},
	plugins: [precompile.rspack()]
}
```

**esbuild**

```ts
import { precompile } from "@ark/precompile/unplugin"
import { build } from "esbuild"

await build({
	entryPoints: ["src/main.ts"],
	// required, as precompiled modules import validators the bundle includes
	bundle: true,
	outfile: "dist/main.js",
	plugins: [precompile.esbuild()]
})
```

**Others**

Rsbuild takes `precompile.rsbuild()`, Bun's bundler `precompile.bun()` and Farm `precompile.farm()`.

By default, each definition becomes a standalone validator and `arktype` resolves to `arktype/runtime`. A dependency that imports `arktype` gets `arktype/runtime` too, where defining a Type throws, so the build fails for each such package unless it [opts in](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#libraries).

## Next

With Turbopack, add the loader as a rule for each extension your definitions and config module are in, and alias arktype's entries to the runtime:

```js
export default {
	turbopack: {
		rules: {
			"*.ts": { loaders: ["@ark/precompile/turbopack"] },
			"*.tsx": { loaders: ["@ark/precompile/turbopack"] }
		},
		resolveAlias: {
			arktype: "arktype/runtime",
			"arktype/codecs": "arktype/runtime",
			"arktype/config": "arktype/runtime",
			"arktype/errors": "arktype/runtime",
			"arktype/mutatesInput": "arktype/runtime"
		}
	}
}
```

The loader fails a module whose `arktype` imports resolve otherwise, naming the aliases to add. With `runtime: "arktype"` or `shadow: true`, leave the aliases out, since the loader fails a module they resolve to the runtime. It reruns when a module's local imports change, and applies a changed configuration once the dev server restarts.

With webpack (`next build --webpack`), add the plugin:

```js
import { precompile } from "@ark/precompile/unplugin"

export default {
	webpack: config => {
		config.plugins.push(precompile.webpack())
		return config
	}
}
```

## Test runners and runtimes

Vitest uses the Vite plugin. For the others, each driver takes the plugin's options, fails on the same errors and resolves `arktype` to `arktype/runtime` where its host allows. The precompiler runs in a worker thread, sharing no module state with your program.

Node 22.15 or later, for `node --test` or any program (pass `--enable-source-maps` for original lines in stack traces):

```ts
// run with `node --import ./register.ts --test`
import { register } from "@ark/precompile/node"

register()
```

Bun, for `bun test` or any program, from a file listed in `preload` in `bunfig.toml`:

```ts
import { precompile } from "@ark/precompile/bun"

Bun.plugin(precompile())
```

Bun doesn't ask a runtime plugin to resolve packages, so `arktype` resolves to the runtime `cwd` resolves for every importer, and dependencies aren't checked for copies of arktype.

To test that your precompiled validators behave as arktype does, run tests in [shadow mode](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#shadow-mode).

## Check an existing project

`--check` lists the definitions that can't be precompiled, and why, without bundling:

```sh
npx arktype-precompile --check "src/**/*.ts"
```

```
src/forms.ts:5:21  accepted
src/forms.ts:14:19  type(`string <= ${limit}`) cannot be precompiled
  `limit` is a parameter of makeField (src/forms.ts:12:22); its value is known only at runtime
  Standalone builds construct every Type at build time. Make it static, or build with runtime: "arktype".
```

It takes each option that changes what a build refuses, like `--errors none` or `--members '{"assert":false}'`. `--fail-under <percent>` exits with 1 if less than that percent of definitions can be precompiled, or on an error outside a definition, so CI can hold a project to it while it migrates.

The same analysis is available as `new Precompiler(host).analyze(source, id)` from `@ark/precompile`.

## ESLint

The ESLint rule reports what the build would, as you edit:

```js
import { configs } from "@ark/precompile/eslint"

export default [configs.recommended]
```

# Validators

> What a precompiled Type is, and how it differs from one arktype creates

## Standalone validators

In a standalone build, each Type your program defines becomes a validator running on `arktype/runtime`. Call it, `.assert()` with it or pass it as a [Standard Schema](https://arktype.io/docs/standard-schema), as you would the Type:

```ts
// bundled as a validator
export const User = type({ name: "string > 0" })

const out = User(data)

if (out instanceof type.errors) console.error(out.summary)
```

Scopes, Modules, Generics, cyclic Types, `match`, `type.fn` and [codecs](https://arktype.io/docs/codecs) are precompiled too. A Module becomes a plain object of its validators, and a Scope or Generic an empty object, since resolving an alias or instantiating a Generic needs arktype. A call to `define`, which returns its argument, is replaced by the argument.

A definition holding functions, like a narrow, a morph or a class, becomes a call to a factory passing each one where the definition was written. The factory checks at creation that each class, and each function another module supplies, is what its code was compiled for, and throws if not.

## What a validator has

Besides being called, a validator has `allows()`, and by default `assert()`, `meta`, `~standard`, `traverse()`, `from()` and `toString()`. `expression`, `description`, `json`, `toJSON()`, `toJsonSchema()` and `~standard.jsonSchema` ship only where the build's [`members`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#members) option sets them, baked as arktype returns them. A read the build sees, like `User.expression`, is replaced by its value either way.

It lacks the methods that compose or relate a Type, like `.and`, `.or`, `.in` or `.extends`. The build fails where it sees one read outside a definition it precompiles, including off a value it lost track of after a Type reached it, and, once for each import, off an import it can't resolve, like one only a bundler alias names:

```
main.ts:8:29  Long.description reads description, which a standalone validator lacks
  `Long` is a Type, which the standalone runtime replaces with a validator, and no precompiled site covers the read
  Standalone builds do not ship arktype. Use it inside a precompiled definition, or build with runtime: "arktype".
```

Composing inside a definition is fine, since the build evaluates it: `export const Admin = User.and({ role: "'admin'" })` is precompiled to a validator of its own. So is [`.encode`](https://arktype.io/docs/codecs) wherever the build sees it read, like `const encode = (event: unknown) => Event.encode(event)`: the encoder is precompiled like any other Type, and receives each codec's `encode` function from the validator holding it.

A validator and its members are frozen, except a Date or RegExp it holds, unless the build sets [`freeze: false`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#freeze).

## Errors

A validator returns errors of its own, instances of `type.errors` and of `arktype`'s `ArkErrors`. Each issue holds the failed check's `code`, `path`, `data` and `expected`, with a message like `name must be a string`:

- A message doesn't say what the value was unless text configured for it does, and the errors arktype groups at one path stay apart. A union no branch allows is one issue.
- A path starting with an index reads `[0] must be a string`, without arktype's `value at`, even where a problem is configured.
- Text a narrow or morph puts in `ctx.reject({ meta })` isn't written, so pass it as `expected`, `problem` or `message` instead.
- A validator a morph calls with its `ctx` adds its issues to that validation.
- `arktype/runtime` doesn't export `byPath`, `flatByPath`, `flatProblemsByPath`, `byAncestorPath` or `messageIn`, and the errors have no `toLocaleString`.
- A `message`, `problem`, `expected` or `actual` configured for a code or on a Type is written as arktype writes it. A build configured with what a validator can't write, like a locale, [fails with its fix](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#configuration).
- They aren't instances of `@ark/schema`'s `ArkErrors`, so the build fails where a module imports that one.

The [`errors`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#errors) option ships less: one issue, or one saying the data is invalid.

## Shipping arktype instead

`runtime: "arktype"` ships arktype, leaving definitions as written: each stays a Type with its whole API, and the build registers the code arktype would compile for it, so it skips compiling at runtime. A definition the build can't precompile is compiled at runtime as usual. Use it while you migrate, or where a program relies on composing Types at runtime.

```ts
precompile.vite({ runtime: "arktype" })
```

To leave only some definitions to arktype in a standalone build, mark them as [runtime islands](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#runtime-islands).

## Limits

- The build doesn't see a Type reach a value through `arguments`, a generator, `Reflect.get`, `import()` or a namespace read at a runtime key, nor a direct `eval` or `with` changing a binding a definition reads. A Type it never sees reach a value is missed: calling a member it lacks throws, and reading one reads `undefined`.
- A definition whose branches arktype orders by the names of the functions they hold, like `type.instanceOf(Cat).or(type.instanceOf(Dog))`, is reported, since a minifier can rename them.
- A definition holding a function a parameter holds, or resolving a Scope alias a thunk defines whose Type holds one, is reported. Mark it as a [runtime island](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#runtime-islands).
- A union whose branches print alike once their functions are named prints as `X or X` where arktype prints `X`.
- A Date or RegExp a Type holds is one object for every Type and validation holding it.
- A builtin class a Type holds, like `Uint8Array`, is read as the validator's module loads, so a later polyfill isn't seen.
- When a validator rejects an array, it may look for errors only from the first element it rejects, so a getter or `Proxy` trap reading an element before that one runs once rather than twice.
- The `ctx.config` a narrow or morph receives holds only `jitless` and `onFail`.
- A module of validators fails to link to an `arktype/runtime` of another version, but nothing checks at runtime that `arktype` loads only for runtime islands.

# Options

> Ship less, and configure a precompiled program

A standalone build can leave out what your program doesn't need. Every option goes to the plugin, a driver or the CLI:

```ts
precompile.vite({
	errors: "none",
	mutatesInput: "always",
	members: { assert: false }
})
```

`errors`, `mutatesInput`, `members`, `optimize`, `freeze`, `lazy`, `checks` and `countsKeys` take effect in standalone mode alone, so setting one with `runtime: "arktype"` fails the build.

### errors

`errors: "first"` stops each validation at the first issue it finds and returns it alone. Which of the data's issues that is isn't promised: the validator looks for whichever is cheapest to find, which may not be the one arktype finds first. `errors: "none"` returns errors holding one root issue with the code `"predicate"` and the message `is invalid`, so no check's description or message ships. Those errors have no `throw()`, and `assert` throws a plain `Error` whose `cause` is the errors.

The plugin and the Node and Bun drivers resolve `@ark/schema/runtime` to `@ark/schema/runtime/none` under `errors: "none"`, and a module importing any other `@ark/schema` entry, or a runtime island, fails the build. Turbopack needs an alias beside [the ones a standalone build needs](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#next):

```js
export default {
	turbopack: {
		resolveAlias: { "@ark/schema/runtime": "@ark/schema/runtime/none" }
	}
}
```

The values are [arktype's `errors`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#errors) option's, and a program that also configures it must configure the same value.

### mutatesInput

`mutatesInput: true` or `"always"` writes what a validation transforms into its input and returns it, as [arktype's option](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#mutatesinput) does. A program that also configures it must configure the same value.

### members

`members` decides what a validator has besides validating. `assert`, `meta`, `~standard`, `methods` (`traverse()`, `from()` and `toString()`) and `errorMethods` default to true; `expression`, `description`, `json`, `toJSON`, `toJsonSchema` and `~standard.jsonSchema` default to false. A dropped member reads `undefined`, and the build fails where it sees the program read one, like `User.assert(data)` or `String(User)`.

Each introspection member set true is baked as arktype returns it under the program's configuration, and `toJsonSchema()` then takes only a `target`. A JSON Schema the build can't bake throws where it's read.

```ts
precompile.vite({
	members: { assert: false, toJsonSchema: true, "~standard.jsonSchema": true }
})
```

`members: { errorMethods: false }` gives errors only their `count`, `issues` and `summary`. They lack `throw()`, `toJSON()` and `toString()`, so `JSON.stringify` writes their internals, though `instanceof type.errors` still recognizes them. `.assert()` still throws a `TraversalError`. They're the smallest errors a build can return, and reading their issues is slower.

The build loads `@ark/schema/runtime/lean` in place of `@ark/schema/runtime` for it, or `@ark/schema/runtime/none-lean` with `errors: "none"`, and a runtime island fails the build, as under [`errors: "none"`](#errors). With Turbopack, alias `@ark/schema/runtime` to that entry as `errors: "none"` does.

### optimize

`optimize: "size"` writes validators for size rather than speed. They're then slower, most where one calls several others in turn, so prefer it where bundle size matters more than validation speed.

### countsKeys

`countsKeys: true` checks a Type that rejects undeclared keys by counting an object's own enumerable keys, as most validators do, instead of checking each key against the declared ones. It counts only on a plain object, meaning one whose prototype is `Object.prototype`. If the count differs from the number of declared keys the object holds, or the object isn't plain, the validator checks each key as before. Errors are unaffected: a validation that fails reports each undeclared key. Index signatures and tuples are still checked key by key, and an `optimize: "size"` build counts nothing.

What it gives up: an undeclared key can pass in place of a declared key that a plain object holds as a non-enumerable property or inherits from `Object.prototype`. For example, `{ "+": "reject", toString: "Function" }` passes `{ extra: 1 }`.

### freeze

`freeze: false` leaves validators and their members unfrozen. Otherwise, writing to one throws in strict mode code.

### lazy

`lazy: false` creates each validator as its module loads rather than where it's first read, so an error creating one throws on import.

### checks

`checks` decides what a factory checks of what it receives: `"types"` (the default) checks each Type, Module, Scope and Generic is the one the build read, `"helpers"` (the default where Vitest runs tests) each static helper too, and `"none"` only those holding functions, so a module mock replacing any other goes unnoticed.

### allowUnsafe

`allowUnsafe: true` (`--allow-unsafe` for `--check`) reports as warnings the problems that may throw at runtime but that a build can still write output for: a dependency that imports arktype or ships precompiled validators, a module the build can't precompile importing arktype, a read off an import it can't resolve, an import that loads a Type before the config module, and a definition that throws a ParseError. Each fails the build otherwise. It applies with `runtime: "arktype"` too, where a ParseError and a dependency shipping precompiled validators fail the build and the rest are warnings anyway.

### conditions and tsconfig

`conditions` and `tsconfig` set the export conditions and the tsconfig whose `paths` the build resolves imports with.

## Configuration

A program that calls `configure()` does so once, in a module imported before any that defines a Type, and names it as the build's `config`:

```ts
import { configure } from "arktype/config"

configure({
	onUndeclaredKey: "delete",
	onFail: errors => errors.throw()
})
```

```ts
precompile.vite({ config: "./config.ts" })
```

The build evaluates the argument, which must be static, and precompiles every definition under it. `onFail` can be any function.

A `message`, `problem`, `expected` or `actual` configured for a code, or on a Type with `.configure()` or its meta, as a string or a function, is written as arktype writes it. What a standalone validator can't write fails the build, each with its fix:

- a locale
- a function writing a union's or a discriminated union's text, which arktype passes each branch's errors: configure the text as a string
- text a Scope configures for a code: configure it with `configure()`, or on each Type with `.configure()`
- `predicate` text from `configure()` where a narrow or morph raises the error: pass the text to `ctx.reject()`

The build fails where a module that creates a Type is imported before the config module, and the runtime throws if `configure()` runs after it creates its first validator, runs twice, or receives other values than the build read.

`config: false` says the program never calls `configure()`, so the build fails wherever it does.

A program configuring `errors` or `mutatesInput`, globally or for a Scope, builds with the same value: a definition whose Types are configured otherwise fails the build, naming both.

# Troubleshooting

> What the build reports, and how to fix it

A build that precompiles everything is quiet. Otherwise, each problem is reported in the same shape: where it is, what the build couldn't do, why, and how to fix it.

```
src/forms.ts:14:19  type(`string <= ${limit}`) cannot be precompiled
  `limit` is a parameter of makeField (src/forms.ts:12:22); its value is known only at runtime
  Standalone builds construct every Type at build time. Make it static, or build with runtime: "arktype".
```

Positions are your source's, even where another plugin transpiled it first. Run [`arktype-precompile --check`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#check-an-existing-project) to see every report at once.

Where the fix is clear and the problem could throw at runtime, the build fails. Where it could still write output, as for a dependency, a read off an import it can't resolve or a definition that throws a ParseError, the hint ends `Set allowUnsafe: true to build anyway, with a warning.` [`allowUnsafe`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#allowunsafe) reports those as warnings instead, and what they report may then throw at runtime. A few reports are always warnings, since the build can't be sure of a fix or nothing fails at runtime: a value the build can't follow that it takes for a Standard Schema other than a Type, like a Zod schema, and what a build with `runtime: "arktype"` leaves to arktype.

## Definitions

**`... cannot be precompiled`**: the definition reads a value known only at runtime, like a parameter or the result of a call the build can't evaluate. Make the value static, mark the definition as a [runtime island](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#runtime-islands), or build with `runtime: "arktype"`.

**`... can't be precompiled yet`**: the definition uses something the build doesn't support yet. Build it as a runtime island, or with `runtime: "arktype"`.

**`arktype runs this callback while defining the type`**: a callback arktype calls during definition, rather than during validation, must be a static helper the build can compute: one expression or one `return`.

**`` `f` can run before `B` (...) is set; export `B` so the site can receive it ``**: an import cycle can reach the definition before a binding it reads is set. Export the binding.

**`... throws a ParseError`**: the definition is invalid, like an intersection that can never be satisfied, so the build fails, with `runtime: "arktype"` too. Fix the definition. Under `allowUnsafe` it's a warning, and the definition throws the same ParseError at runtime, as a test expecting one means it to.

**`` `// @ark-runtime` marks nothing ``**, **`` `const x = 1` is marked // @ark-runtime but doesn't use arktype ``** or **`... is marked // @ark-runtime inside a definition the build precompiles`**: a [runtime island](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#runtime-islands) marker that leaves nothing to arktype, since nothing follows it, what follows doesn't use arktype, or it's inside a definition the build precompiles. Put `// @ark-runtime` right before a definition arktype should run, or remove it. `allowUnsafe` doesn't change this.

## Reads

**`` `type` is used outside a precompiled site ``**: a standalone build doesn't ship arktype, so a call that creates a Type must be a definition the build precompiles. Move it into one, or build with `runtime: "arktype"`.

**`User.description reads description, which a standalone validator lacks`**: a validator lacks the methods that compose a Type and the introspection members its build's [`members`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#members) option doesn't set. Compose inside a definition, set the member, or build with `runtime: "arktype"`.

**`` `User` comes from `~/schemas`, which the build can't resolve ``**: the build resolves imports as TypeScript does, so it can't check reads off an import only a bundler alias resolves. Add the alias to `tsconfig.json`'s `paths`, or name that tsconfig as the build's `tsconfig`. If the value isn't a Type, annotate it with its type.

## Setup

**`arktype resolves to 2.3.0, but @ark/precompile runs on 2.2.9`**: validators run only on the arktype they were built with. Install one version, e.g. with your package manager's dedupe or overrides.

**`precompiledForArktype_2_2_9` is not exported by `arktype/runtime`** (each bundler words it its own way): every module of validators imports an export of `arktype/runtime` named for the version it was built for, so linking it to another version's runtime fails rather than misbehaving at runtime. It usually means a bundler cache from before an upgrade, or a second copy of arktype. Install one version and clear the bundler's cache.

**`arktype resolves to more than one copy`**: one copy doesn't recognize another's Types and errors. The message names each copy and the file that reached it.

**`arktype resolves to ... rather than arktype/runtime`** (Turbopack): add the `turbopack.resolveAlias` entries the message lists to your Next config. See [Next](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#next).

**`configure() is called, but the build has no config module`**: name the module that calls it as the build's [`config`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#configuration).

**`... loads src/schemas.ts, which creates a Type, before the config module src/config.ts runs configure()`**: creating that Type would throw unless the program loaded the config module earlier. Import the config module first, before any module that creates a Type.

**`precompile.esbuild() needs bundle: true`**: precompiled modules import validators the bundle includes.

**`my-schemas imports arktype, which a standalone build resolves to arktype/runtime, where defining a Type throws`**: a dependency defines Types at runtime. Have it publish its source and [opt in](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#libraries) with `"arktype": { "precompile": true }` in its `package.json`, so your build precompiles it.

**`my-schemas imports arktype/runtime, so it ships validators precompiled for one version of arktype`**: a dependency shipped its own precompiled build, which runs only on the arktype it was built with. Have it publish its source and opt in instead.

**`src/Form.svelte imports arktype, which a standalone build resolves to arktype/runtime`**: the build can't precompile a module that isn't JavaScript or TypeScript, like a Svelte component's script. Define the Types it uses in a module that is.

**`... was written by a build whose cache kept it in ..., where it no longer is`**: delete the bundler's cache to rebuild.

# Advanced

> Shadow mode, libraries, runtime islands and declarations

## Shadow mode

`shadow: true` makes a test suite tell where a standalone build would behave otherwise than arktype. Each definition is precompiled and also created by arktype from the same values, and the program runs on arktype, only `arktype/config` resolving to the runtime:

```ts
import { precompile } from "@ark/precompile/unplugin"
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config"

export default defineConfig({ plugins: [precompile.vite({ shadow: true })] })
```

Each Type, Module and `type.fn` compares its validator with arktype's as it's created, as it validates (by result, the input it leaves and each call to a function the program passed) and as its members are read. Where they agree, it returns arktype's result. Where they don't, it throws an error naming the definition, what was observed and both results, and raises it again where a fallback or `expect(...).toThrow()` can't catch it.

During a validation, each function a definition holds runs once, its calls and plain writes to its arguments replayed for the validator. A call that adds an error to `ctx` or writes otherwise, like setting a `Date`'s time, runs again for the validator, which must answer alike.

## Libraries

A library ships its source, and the build precompiles it with the program if its `package.json` opts in:

```json
{
	"name": "my-schemas",
	"arktype": { "precompile": true }
}
```

Its definitions are then precompiled like the program's. The plugin and drivers find such packages through the dependencies of the nearest `package.json` to `cwd` and of each package that opts in, and the plugin keeps Vite and Vitest from prebundling or externalizing them.

A library shouldn't ship what its own build precompiled, which runs only on the arktype it was built with, so the build fails for each dependency that imports `arktype/runtime`.

## Runtime islands

In a standalone build, a definition can be left to arktype by marking it:

```ts
// @ark-runtime
export const Shaped = type(await loadShape())
```

The marker applies to the statement or expression after it. arktype then ships beside `arktype/runtime` for the modules with islands alone. The build fails if an island reads a precompiled validator other than to validate with it, or reaches arktype outside an island, e.g. through a helper in another module. It fails too for a marker that leaves nothing to arktype: one nothing follows, one on code that doesn't use arktype, or one inside a definition the build precompiles. `--check` leaves islands out of its rate.

## Declarations

A package whose types others read can declare its Types once, so its consumers don't infer arktype definitions:

```sh
npx arktype-precompile --declare
```

This writes what `tsc --emitDeclarationOnly` would for the nearest `tsconfig.json`, or the one `--tsconfig` names, except that each Type, Scope and Module is declared through its shape in one `~arktype.d.ts` at the declarations' root, named once and referenced wherever another shape holds it:

```ts
// users.d.ts
export declare const User: import("arktype").Type<import("./~arktype.js").User>

// ~arktype.d.ts
export type User = {
	id: string
	role: import("arktype").Default<Role, "member">
	address?: Address | undefined
}
```

A consumer's type-check then reads each Type's shape rather than inferring its definition. A shape TypeScript can't name where a consumer resolves it, like a class its module doesn't export, is left to TypeScript's own declaration. The CLI exits with 1 where TypeScript reports an error, after writing what it emitted.

The bundler plugin emits the same files with a Rollup, Rolldown, Vite, webpack, Rspack or Rsbuild build that neither watches nor serves:

```ts
precompile.vite({ declare: true })
```

esbuild, Bun, Farm and the Node and Turbopack drivers can't tell whether a build watches, so `declare: true` throws there; run `arktype-precompile --declare` after the build instead.

Declarations read the compiler API of TypeScript 5.5 to 6 from the optional `typescript` peer. A TypeScript 7 project installs TypeScript 6 beside it:

```sh
npm i -D typescript-6@npm:typescript@6
```

# Dynamic vs Precompiled

> The same definitions, run two ways

Every ArkType definition can run dynamically, created by `type()` at runtime, or [precompiled](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile), constructed when you build. Your definitions and their inferred types are identical either way, so you can switch at any time.

- Runtime (instructions per call, lower is better): moltar's parseSafe benchmark (validate, removing undeclared keys), instructions per call, Node 24. Source: moltar/typescript-runtime-type-benchmarks, https\://moltar.github.io/typescript-runtime-type-benchmarks/
- ArkType (precompiled): 189
- @ts-runtypes: 209
- Typia: 213
- ata-validator (AOT): 220
- ArkType (dynamic): 262

* Bundle size (B gzipped, lower is better): valibot.dev's login form, each reporting every error with a message; precompiled with its validator's members and methods, and its errors' methods, off. Source: valibot.dev's comparison, https\://valibot.dev/guides/comparison/
* ArkType (precompiled): 912
* Valibot: 1,475
* Zod Mini: 5,127
* Zod: 25,058
* ArkType (dynamic): 75,520

Precompiled ArkType is the fastest on moltar's parseSafe and assertLoose benchmarks, and on Valibot's own login form it reports every error, with its message, in a smaller bundle than Valibot. The charts come from different builds: each names its benchmark and the options it was built with.

Validating valid data, the two modes run the same checks. On schemabenchmarks.dev's product schema, dynamic ArkType validates valid data as fast as precompiled ArkType. What precompiling removes is everything around those checks: the parser, the time it takes to create each Type, and the code it generates.

| | Dynamic | Precompiled | Precompiled with `runtime: "arktype"` |
| - | - | - | - |
| Build step | none | a bundler plugin or driver | a bundler plugin or driver |
| Ships arktype's parser | yes | no, only `arktype/runtime` | yes |
| Generates code at runtime | yes, unless [`jitless`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#jitless) | never | only for Types the build couldn't precompile |
| Composing at runtime | the whole Type API | inside definitions, which the build evaluates | the whole Type API |
| Introspection members | all | those the [`members`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#members) option bakes | all |
| Error messages | say what was expected and what the value was | say what was expected, and any text configured for them | say what was expected and what the value was |
| [Locales](https://arktype.io/docs/i18n) | yes | no | yes |

## Which to use

Precompile an app you bundle. Its validators ship without a parser or a JIT, and the build reports anything it can't precompile with the fix, which is a quick loop when an agent runs your local dev. See [Setup](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup).

Stay dynamic where there's no build, like a script or a REPL, or where definitions are only known at runtime. A standalone build can also leave those to arktype as [runtime islands](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#runtime-islands).

Build with `runtime: "arktype"` while you migrate, or where a program composes or introspects Types at runtime but still benefits from skipping the compile step.

# Primitives

> Define strings, numbers, bigints, symbols, booleans, null and undefined, with literals, patterns, lengths, ranges and divisors.

## string

### keywords

Reference a keyword anywhere a definition is expected:

```ts
const User = type({
	email: "string.email",
	ids: "string.uuid.v4[]"
})
```

| Alias | Description |
| - | - |
| `string` | a string |
| `string.alpha` | only letters |
| `string.alphanumeric` | only letters and digits 0-9 |
| `string.base58` | base58-encoded |
| `string.base64` | base64-encoded |
| `string.base64.url` | base64url-encoded |
| `string.capitalize` | a morph from a string to capitalized |
| `string.capitalize.preformatted` | capitalized |
| `string.creditCard` | a credit card number and a credit card number |
| `string.date` | a string and a parsable date |
| `string.date.epoch` | an integer string representing a safe Unix timestamp |
| `string.date.epoch.parse` | a morph from an integer string representing a safe Unix timestamp to a Date |
| `string.date.iso` | an ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.sssZ) date |
| `string.date.iso.parse` | a morph from an ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.sssZ) date to a Date |
| `string.date.parse` | a morph from a string and a parsable date to a Date |
| `string.digits` | only digits 0-9 |
| `string.email` | an email address |
| `string.hex` | hex characters only |
| `string.integer` | a well-formed integer string |
| `string.integer.parse` | a morph from a well-formed integer string to an integer |
| `string.ip` | an IP address |
| `string.ip.v4` | an IPv4 address |
| `string.ip.v6` | an IPv6 address |
| `string.json` | a JSON string |
| `string.json.parse` | safe JSON string parser |
| `string.lower` | a morph from a string to only lowercase letters |
| `string.lower.preformatted` | only lowercase letters |
| `string.normalize` | a morph from a string to NFC-normalized unicode |
| `string.normalize.NFC` | a morph from a string to NFC-normalized unicode |
| `string.normalize.NFC.preformatted` | NFC-normalized unicode |
| `string.normalize.NFD` | a morph from a string to NFD-normalized unicode |
| `string.normalize.NFD.preformatted` | NFD-normalized unicode |
| `string.normalize.NFKC` | a morph from a string to NFKC-normalized unicode |
| `string.normalize.NFKC.preformatted` | NFKC-normalized unicode |
| `string.normalize.NFKD` | a morph from a string to NFKD-normalized unicode |
| `string.normalize.NFKD.preformatted` | NFKD-normalized unicode |
| `string.numeric` | a well-formed numeric string |
| `string.numeric.parse` | a morph from a well-formed numeric string to a number |
| `string.regex` | a string and a regex pattern |
| `string.semver` | a semantic version (see https\://semver.org/) |
| `string.trim` | a morph from a string to trimmed |
| `string.trim.preformatted` | trimmed |
| `string.upper` | a morph from a string to only uppercase letters |
| `string.upper.preformatted` | only uppercase letters |
| `string.url` | a string and a URL string |
| `string.url.parse` | a morph from a string and a URL string to a URL instance |
| `string.uuid` | a UUID |
| `string.uuid.v1` | a UUIDv1 |
| `string.uuid.v2` | a UUIDv2 |
| `string.uuid.v3` | a UUIDv3 |
| `string.uuid.v4` | a UUIDv4 |
| `string.uuid.v5` | a UUIDv5 |
| `string.uuid.v6` | a UUIDv6 |
| `string.uuid.v7` | a UUIDv7 |
| `string.uuid.v8` | a UUIDv8 |

Every keyword, including those for other types, is listed on the [keywords](https://arktype.io/docs/keywords) page.

### literals

Quote a string inside a definition to allow exactly that string. Single and double quotes are equivalent:

```ts
const Literals = type({
	singleQuoted: "'typescript'",
	doubleQuoted: '"arktype"'
})
```

### patterns

A regex literal requires the string to match it. Like a `RegExp`, it is unanchored unless you anchor it with `^` and `$`.

**string**

```ts
const AToZ = type("/^a.*z$/")

// ArkErrors: must be matched by ^a.*z$ (was "abc")
AToZ("abc")
```

**fluent**

```ts
const AToZ = type.string.matching(/^a.*z$/)

// ArkErrors: must be matched by ^a.*z$ (was "abc")
AToZ("abc")
```

A `RegExp` works as a definition too, e.g. `type({ code: /^a.*z$/ })`.

Regex literals are typed with [ArkRegex](https://arktype.io/docs/regex), so a pattern that constrains the string's shape narrows the inferred type:

```ts
// Type<string>
const Hex = type("/^[0-9a-fA-F]+$/")

// Type<`${number}.${number}.${number}`>
const Semver = type("/^(\\d+)\\.(\\d+)\\.(\\d+)$/")
```

#### e(x)ec mode

Prefix a regex literal with `x` to transform the string into the result of `RegExp.prototype.exec`. The output is the match, not the string, and its capture groups are typed:

```ts
const User = type({
	birthday: "x/^(?<month>\\d{2})-(?<day>\\d{2})-(?<year>\\d{4})$/"
})

const data = User.assert({ birthday: "05-21-1993" })

data.birthday.groups.month // "05"
data.birthday.groups.year // "1993"
```

### lengths

Constrain a string's length with `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=` or `==`:

**string**

```ts
const Bounded = type({
	nonEmpty: "string > 0",
	atMost10: "string <= 10",
	exactly5: "string == 5"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Bounded = type({
	nonEmpty: type.string.moreThanLength(0),
	atMost10: type.string.atMostLength(10),
	exactly5: type.string.exactlyLength(5)
})
```

A range sets both bounds at once, each inclusive or exclusive:

**string**

```ts
// 4 to 6 digits
const Pin = type("4 <= string.digits <= 6")

// ArkErrors: must be at least length 4 (was 3)
Pin("123")
```

**fluent**

```ts
// 4 to 6 digits
const Pin = type.keywords.string.digits.atLeastLength(4).atMostLength(6)

// ArkErrors: must be at least length 4 (was 3)
Pin("123")
```

## number

`number` rejects `NaN`, `Infinity` and `-Infinity`. Allow them in one type with the `number.NaN`, `number.Infinity` and `number.NegativeInfinity` keywords:

```ts
const MaybeInfinite = type("number | number.Infinity | number.NegativeInfinity")
```

To allow them everywhere, configure [`numberAllowsNaN`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#numberallowsnan) or [`numberAllowsInfinity`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#numberallowsinfinity).

### keywords

```ts
const User = type({
	createdAt: "number.epoch",
	age: "number.integer >= 0"
})
```

| Alias | Description |
| - | - |
| `number` | a number |
| `number.Infinity` | Infinity |
| `number.NaN` | NaN |
| `number.NegativeInfinity` | -Infinity |
| `number.epoch` | an integer representing a safe Unix timestamp |
| `number.integer` | an integer |
| `number.safe` | at least -9007199254740991 and at most 9007199254740991 |

### literals

A number in a definition allows exactly that number:

```ts
const Literals = type({
	number: "1337"
})
```

### ranges

Constrain a number with `>`, `>=`, `<` or `<=`:

**string**

```ts
const Bounded = type({
	positive: "number > 0",
	atMost5: "number <= 5"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Bounded = type({
	positive: type.number.moreThan(0),
	atMost5: type.number.atMost(5)
})
```

A range sets both bounds at once, each inclusive or exclusive:

**string**

```ts
const Percentage = type("0 <= number <= 100")

// ArkErrors: must be at most 100 (was 101)
Percentage(101)
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Percentage = type.number.atLeast(0).atMost(100)

// ArkErrors: must be at most 100 (was 101)
Percentage(101)
```

### divisors

Constrain a number to a multiple of an integer with `%`:

**string**

```ts
const Even = type("number % 2")

// ArkErrors: must be even (was 3)
Even(3)
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Even = type.number.divisibleBy(2)

// ArkErrors: must be even (was 3)
Even(3)
```

## bigint

**string**

```ts
const Bigints = type({
	foo: "bigint"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Bigints = type({
	foo: type.bigint
})
```

### literals

Add the suffix `n` to a [number literal](https://arktype.io/docs/primitives#number-literals) to allow exactly that `bigint`:

```ts
const Literals = type({
	bigint: "1337n"
})
```

A [unit expression](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#unit) like `type.unit(1337n)` does the same.

## symbol

**string**

```ts
const Symbols = type({
	key: "symbol"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Symbols = type({
	key: type.symbol
})
```

To allow one specific symbol, use a [unit expression](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#unit).

Symbol keys need no special syntax, e.g. `{ [mySymbol]: "string" }`. See [properties](https://arktype.io/docs/objects#properties) to make them optional or defaultable.

## boolean

**string**

```ts
const Booleans = type({
	key: "boolean"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Booleans = type({
	key: type.boolean
})
```

### literals

**string**

```ts
const Booleans = type({
	a: "true",
	b: "false",
	// equivalent to "boolean"
	c: "true | false"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Booleans = type({
	a: type.true,
	b: type.false,
	// equivalent to type.boolean
	c: type.true.or(type.false)
})
```

## null

`"null"` allows exactly `null`, usually in a [union](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#union):

**string**

```ts
const MyObj = type({
	foo: "number | null"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const MyObj = type({
	foo: type.number.or(type.null)
})
```

## undefined

`"undefined"` allows exactly `undefined`, usually in a [union](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#union):

**string**

```ts
const MyObj = type({
	requiredKey: "number | undefined",
	"optionalKey?": "number | undefined"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const MyObj = type({
	requiredKey: type.number.or(type.undefined),
	optionalKey: type.number.or(type.undefined).optional()
})
```

> **Allowing undefined does not make a key optional**
>
> Like in TypeScript, a required key that allows `undefined` must still be present:
>
> ```ts
> const MyObj = type({
> 	key: "number | undefined"
> })
>
> // { key: undefined }
> MyObj({ key: undefined })
>
> // ArkErrors: key must be a number or undefined (was missing)
> MyObj({})
> ```

# Objects

> Define objects, arrays, tuples, dates and class instances, and derive new object types from existing ones.

## properties

An object definition can combine required, optional and defaultable keys with index signatures.

### required

**string**

```ts
const symbolicKey = Symbol()

const MyObj = type({
	requiredKey: "string",
	// nested definitions don't need their own type call
	[symbolicKey]: {
		nested: "unknown"
	}
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const symbolicKey = Symbol()

const MyObj = type({
	requiredKey: type.string,
	// nested definitions don't need their own type call
	[symbolicKey]: {
		nested: type.unknown
	}
})
```

### optional

**string**

```ts
const symbolicKey = Symbol()

const MyObj = type({
	"optionalKey?": "number[]",
	[symbolicKey]: "string?"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const symbolicKey = Symbol()

const MyObj = type({
	optionalKey: type.number.array().optional(),
	[symbolicKey]: type.string.optional()
})
```

**tuple**

```ts
const symbolicKey = Symbol()

const MyObj = type({
	optionalKey: ["number[]", "?"],
	[symbolicKey]: ["string", "?"]
})
```

> **Key or value syntax?**
>
> Prefer the key syntax, `"key?"`. It mirrors TypeScript and reads as what it is: a constraint on whether the key is present, not on its value.
>
> Put `?` on the value when the key is a symbol, when you want go-to-definition and JSDoc on an unquoted key, or when you'd rather not quote keys.

> **An optional key doesn't allow undefined**
>
> ArkType checks optional keys the way TypeScript does with [`exactOptionalPropertyTypes`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig#exactOptionalPropertyTypes): a missing key is valid, but a key set to `undefined` must allow `undefined`.
>
> ```ts
> const MyObj = type({
> 	"key?": "number"
> })
>
> // {}
> MyObj({})
>
> // ArkErrors: key must be a number (was undefined)
> MyObj({ key: undefined })
> ```
>
> To allow it, add `undefined` to the value: `"key?": "number | undefined"`. You can also set [`exactOptionalPropertyTypes`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#exactoptionalpropertytypes) to `false` globally.

### defaultable

A defaultable key is optional in the input. When it is missing, the output has its default.

**string**

```ts
const MyObj = type({
	defaultableKey: "boolean = false"
})

// { defaultableKey: false }
MyObj({})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const MyObj = type({
	defaultableKey: type.boolean.default(false)
})

// { defaultableKey: false }
MyObj({})
```

**tuple**

```ts
const MyObj = type({
	defaultableKey: ["boolean", "=", false]
})

// { defaultableKey: false }
MyObj({})
```

`= []` and `= {}` give each output its own new array or object, so mutating one never changes another:

```ts
const MyObj = type({
	values: "string[] = []",
	meta: "object = {}"
})
```

For any other object, default to a function that returns it, e.g. `type.Date.default(() => new Date())`.

> **Optional and default only work in objects and tuples**
>
> `number.optional()` and `number.default(0)` don't return a `Type`. They return the tuple definitions `[Type<number>, "?"]` and `[Type<number>, "=", 0]`, which are only valid as a property or a tuple element. `type("string?")` throws a `ParseError`.
>
> For a `Type` that accepts `undefined`, use a union like `type("string | undefined")`. To replace `undefined` with a value, add a morph:
>
> ```ts
> const FallbackString = type("string | undefined").pipe(v => v ?? "")
> ```

### index

An index signature constrains every key that matches it:

```ts
const Scores = type({
	"[string]": "number"
})
```

The key can be any string or symbol type, like `symbol`, `string | symbol`, a keyword like `string.uuid` or a regex literal:

```ts
const DataAttributes = type({
	"[/^data-/]": "string"
})

// ArkErrors: value at ["data-id"] must be a string (was a number)
DataAttributes({ "data-id": 1 })
```

A union of literal keys becomes those named keys, so `"['a' | 'b']": "number"` is `{ a: number, b: number }`.

`Record` is available as a [generic keyword](https://arktype.io/docs/generics#keywords), e.g. `type("Record<string, number>")` or `type.Record("string", "number")`.

### undeclared

By default, ArkType allows keys you didn't declare, like TypeScript does. That lets you validate an object you already have without copying it, and skipping the check for extra keys is faster.

To reject or delete undeclared keys, set `"+"` in the object, or [configure](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#onundeclaredkey) a different default for every object:

**string**

```ts
// fail if any string key other than "onlyAllowedKey" is present
const MyClosedObject = type({
	"+": "reject",
	onlyAllowedKey: "string"
})

// delete every key other than "onlyPreservedKey"
const MyStrippedObject = type({
	"+": "delete",
	onlyPreservedKey: "string"
})

// allow and keep undeclared keys (the default)
const MyOpenObject = type({
	"+": "ignore",
	nonexclusiveKey: "number"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
// fail if any string key other than "onlyAllowedKey" is present
const MyClosedObject = type({
	onlyAllowedKey: "string"
}).onUndeclaredKey("reject")

// delete every key other than "onlyPreservedKey"
const MyStrippedObject = type({
	onlyPreservedKey: "string"
}).onUndeclaredKey("delete")

// allow and keep undeclared keys (the default)
const MyOpenObject = type({
	nonexclusiveKey: "number"
}).onUndeclaredKey("ignore")
```

`"ignore"` only matters if you configured a different default.

A rejected key is an error with the code `undeclared`:

```ts
const MyClosedObject = type({
	"+": "reject",
	onlyAllowedKey: "string"
})

// ArkErrors: extraKey must be removed
MyClosedObject({ onlyAllowedKey: "ok", extraKey: 1 })
```

`"reject"` checks string keys only, so an undeclared symbol key passes, while `"delete"` removes undeclared symbol keys too. Reject types that differ only by a symbol key therefore overlap, and a union of them with a morph is indeterminate.

`"delete"` builds a new object with the declared keys in the order of the type's expression: required keys, then optional keys, each sorted by name.

`.onDeepUndeclaredKey()` applies the same behavior to every nested object:

```ts
const MyDeeplyStrippedObject = type({
	preserved: "string",
	nested: {
		preserved: "string"
	}
}).onDeepUndeclaredKey("delete")

// { nested: { preserved: "b" }, preserved: "a" }
MyDeeplyStrippedObject({
	preserved: "a",
	extra: 1,
	nested: { preserved: "b", extra: 2 }
})
```

> **Prefer in-object syntax where possible**
>
