> `.onUndeclaredKey()` and `.configure()` rebuild the whole type they're called on, so creating a type with them is slower than writing `"+"` in the object. Validation is equally fast either way. Methods like `.or()` and `.pipe()` reference the original type rather than rebuilding it, so they have no such cost.

### merge

Merging adds properties to an object or replaces existing ones, like JavaScript's [spread syntax](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Spread_syntax). Write it as a `"..."` key in the object, `.merge()` or the `Merge` generic:

**string**

```ts
const User = type({ isAdmin: "false", name: "string" })

// Type<{ name: string; isAdmin: true; permissions: string[] }>
const Admin = type({
	"...": User,
	isAdmin: "true",
	permissions: "string[]"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const User = type({ isAdmin: "false", name: "string" })

// Type<{ name: string; isAdmin: true; permissions: string[] }>
const Admin = User.merge({
	isAdmin: "true",
	permissions: "string[]"
})
```

**generic**

```ts
const types = type.module({
	User: { isAdmin: "false", name: "string" },
	AdminProps: { isAdmin: "true", permissions: "string[]" },
	// { name: string; isAdmin: true; permissions: string[] }
	Admin: "Merge<User, AdminProps>"
})
```

A key in both objects takes its value from the merged object. An [intersection](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#intersection) would instead intersect the two values, and `false & true` would throw a `ParseError`. When the keys don't overlap, the two give the same type, but merging is less work to compute, both when the type is created and in your editor, so prefer it for combining properties.

Like the other [structural transformations](https://arktype.io/docs/objects#properties-structural), `merge` builds a new object from the properties, so a root narrow or metadata is not carried over.

#### n-ary

`type.merge` merges any number of objects, each overriding the ones before it:

```ts
// Type<{ b: number; a?: 1 }>
const Merged = type.merge({ a: "string" }, { b: "number" }, { "a?": "1" })
```

### escapes

Escape a key's `?`, or a key that is exactly `+` or `...`, with a backslash to use it literally:

```ts
// Type<{ "isAdmin?": boolean; "+": string }>
const Escaped = type({
	"isAdmin\\?": "boolean",
	"\\+": "string"
})

// ArkErrors: value at ["isAdmin?"] must be boolean (was missing)
Escaped({ "+": "x" })
```

### keyof

Like in TypeScript, `keyof` extracts an object's keys as a union:

**string**

```ts
const types = type.module({
	UsedCar: {
		originallyPurchased: "string.date",
		remainingWheels: "number"
	},
	// "originallyPurchased" | "remainingWheels"
	UsedCarKey: "keyof UsedCar"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const UsedCar = type({
	originallyPurchased: "string.date",
	remainingWheels: "number"
})

// Type<"originallyPurchased" | "remainingWheels">
const UsedCarKey = UsedCar.keyof()
```

**tuple**

```ts
const UsedCar = type({
	originallyPurchased: "string.date",
	remainingWheels: "number"
})

// Type<"originallyPurchased" | "remainingWheels">
const UsedCarKey = type(["keyof", UsedCar])
```

**args**

```ts
const UsedCar = type({
	originallyPurchased: "string.date",
	remainingWheels: "number"
})

// Type<"originallyPurchased" | "remainingWheels">
const UsedCarKey = type("keyof", UsedCar)
```

Also like in TypeScript, a `[string]` index signature absorbs the named keys, so `keyof` is `string`:

```ts
const RecordWithSpecialKeys = type({
	"[string]": "unknown",
	verySpecialKey: "number"
})

// true
RecordWithSpecialKeys.keyof().equals("string")
```

> **ArkType's keyof never includes number**
>
> TypeScript's `keyof` can include `number`, but JavaScript has no numeric keys: `{ 4: true }` and `{ "4": true }` are the same object, and `Object.keys` returns `["4"]` for both. ArkType's `keyof` only returns `string` and `symbol` keys, the two kinds of key an object can have.
>
> **Why ArkType diverges from TypeScript here**
>
> In a set-based type system, two types that describe the same values need the same representation. TypeScript keeps separate numeric and string representations of the same key, which leads to results like this:
>
> ```ts
> type Thing1 = {
> 	[x: string]: unknown
> }
>
> // Thing2 describes the same values as Thing1
> type Thing2 = Record<string, unknown>
>
> type Key1 = keyof Thing1
> // type Key1 = string | number
>
> type Key2 = keyof Thing2
> // type Key2 = string
> ```

### get

Like an indexed access type in TypeScript (`User["name"]`), `get` extracts the type of the value at a key:

```ts
const Manatee = type({
	isFriendly: "true",
	snorf: {
		uses: "string[]"
	}
})

// Type<true>
const IsFriendly = Manatee.get("isFriendly")

// pass more keys to access nested properties
// Type<string[]>
const SnorfUses = Manatee.get("snorf", "uses")
```

The key can also be a union, a literal or an index signature, and the object can be a union with optional keys. The [`get` tests](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/blob/main/ark/type/__tests__/get.test.ts) cover each case.

> **Extracting part of a type can be an antipattern**
>
> Before using `get`, `pick` or `omit` on a type you defined, consider defining that part as its own type and referencing it. Composing small types is usually clearer and faster than extracting parts of a large one.

### structural transformations

`merge`, `pick`, `omit`, `required`, `partial` and `map` each return a **new object built from the properties** of the `Type` they're called on, rather than referencing that `Type`.

> **Only properties are carried over**
>
> Anything attached to the object itself is dropped: most importantly a root [narrow](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#narrow) or [filter](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#filter), but also [metadata](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#metadata) like `.describe(...)`. Constraints on the properties are kept.
>
> ```ts
> const User = type({
> 	name: "string",
> 	email: "string"
> }).narrow(user => user.email.includes("@"))
>
> // the narrow is not a property, so PartialUser doesn't have it
> const PartialUser = User.partial()
>
> // { email: "not an email" }
> PartialUser({ email: "not an email" })
> ```
>
> Reapply what you still need to the result:
>
> ```ts
> const PartialUser = type({
> 	name: "string",
> 	email: "string"
> })
> 	.partial()
> 	.narrow(user => user.email?.includes("@") ?? true)
> ```
>
> A root [morph](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#pipe) can't be reduced to properties, so transforming a type like `type({ name: "string" }).pipe(user => user)` throws a `ParseError` instead of dropping it.

### pick / omit

Keep or remove specific properties:

```ts
const User = type({
	name: "string",
	email: "string.email",
	"age?": "number"
})

// Type<{ name: string; email: string }>
const NameAndEmail = User.pick("name", "email")

// Type<{ name: string; age?: number }>
const WithoutEmail = User.omit("email")
```

In a definition, use the `Pick` and `Omit` [generics](https://arktype.io/docs/generics#keywords). Their keys are definitions, so quote each one:

```ts
const types = type.module({
	User: {
		name: "string",
		email: "string.email",
		"age?": "number"
	},
	NameAndEmail: "Pick<User, 'name' | 'email'>",
	WithoutEmail: "Omit<User, 'email'>"
})
```

### required / partial

Make every named property required or optional:

```ts
const User = type({
	name: "string",
	"email?": "string.email",
	"age?": "number"
})

// Type<{ name: string; email: string; age: number }>
const RequiredUser = User.required()

// Type<{ name?: string; email?: string; age?: number }>
const PartialUser = User.partial()
```

`required` also removes defaults, so a defaulted key becomes a plain required key:

```ts
// Type<{ foo: string }>
const T = type({ foo: "string = 'bar'" }).required()

// ArkErrors: foo must be a string (was missing)
T({})
```

In a definition, use the `Required` and `Partial` [generics](https://arktype.io/docs/generics#keywords), e.g. `"Partial<User>"` in a scope.

> **Arrays and tuples mirror TypeScript's Required and Partial**
>
> Like the mapped types they're named for, `required` and `partial` apply to an array's or tuple's elements:
>
> ```ts
> // Type<[string?, number?]>
> const PartialPair = type(["string", "number"]).partial()
>
> // Type<[string, number]>
> const RequiredPair = type(["string", "number?"]).required()
> ```
>
> They only change whether an element must be present, never the values it allows. TypeScript also adds `undefined` to variadic elements and index signature values, since it has no way to mark them optional. ArkType doesn't, so `type("string[]").partial()` is still `string[]`.
>
> A postfix element can't follow an optional one, in ArkType or in TypeScript, so `partial` throws a `ParseError` on a tuple like `[string, ...number[], boolean]`.

### readonly

Mark every property as `readonly`. This only affects the inferred type; the output isn't frozen.

```ts
// Type<{ readonly id: number; readonly name: string }>
const Frozen = type({
	id: "number",
	name: "string"
}).readonly()
```

### map

`map` transforms each property of an object. The function receives a prop with its `key`, `value` (a `Type`) and `kind` (`"required"` or `"optional"`), and returns a `{ key, value }` object, optionally with `kind`:

```ts
const Name = type({
	first: "string",
	last: "string"
})

// Type<{ first: string | null; last: string | null }>
const NullableName = Name.map(prop => ({
	key: prop.key,
	value: prop.value.or("null")
}))
```

Return `[]` to remove a property, or several props to add more than one:

```ts
const User = type({
	name: "string",
	"age?": "number"
})

// Type<{ name: string }>
const NameOnly = User.map(prop => (prop.key === "age" ? [] : prop))
```

### props

`props` lists an object's properties, with required keys first, then optional keys, each sorted by name:

```ts
const User = type({
	name: "string",
	"age?": "number",
	role: "'admin' | 'user' = 'user'"
})

for (const prop of User.props) {
	console.log(prop.kind) // "required", "optional", "optional"
	console.log(prop.key) // "name", "age", "role"
	console.log(prop.value.expression) // "string", "number", '"admin" | "user"'
	if ("default" in prop) console.log(prop.default) // "user"
}
```

## arrays

**string**

```ts
const Arrays = type({
	key: "string[]"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Arrays = type({
	key: type.string.array()
})
```

**tuple**

```ts
const Arrays = type({
	key: ["string", "[]"]
})
```

**args**

```ts
const Arrays = type({
	key: type("string", "[]")
})
```

### lengths

Constrain an array's length with `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=` or `==`:

**string**

```ts
const Bounded = type({
	nonEmpty: "string[] > 0",
	atMost5: "boolean[] <= 5",
	pair: "number[] == 2"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Bounded = type({
	nonEmpty: type.string.array().moreThanLength(0),
	atMost5: type.boolean.array().atMostLength(5),
	pair: type.number.array().exactlyLength(2)
})
```

A range sets both bounds at once, each inclusive or exclusive:

**string**

```ts
const Tags = type("0 < string[] <= 10")

// ArkErrors: must be non-empty
Tags([])
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Tags = type.string.array().moreThanLength(0).atMostLength(10)

// ArkErrors: must be non-empty
Tags([])
```

## tuples

Like objects, tuples are structures whose values are nested definitions. Like TypeScript, ArkType supports prefix, defaultable, optional, variadic and postfix elements, with the same rules for combining them.

### prefix

**string**

```ts
const MyTuple = type([
	"string",
	// object definitions can be nested in tuples, and vice versa
	{
		coordinates: ["number", "number"]
	}
])
```

**fluent**

```ts
const MyTuple = type([
	type.string,
	// object definitions can be nested in tuples, and vice versa
	{
		coordinates: [type.number, type.number]
	}
])
```

### defaultable

A defaultable element is optional in the input. When it is missing, the output has its default.

Defaultable elements follow the prefix elements and come before any optional elements. Like optional elements, they can't be combined with postfix elements.

**string**

```ts
const MyTuple = type(["string", "boolean = false", "number = 0"])

// ["a", false, 0]
MyTuple(["a"])
```

**fluent**

```ts
const MyTuple = type([
	type.string,
	type.boolean.default(false),
	type.number.default(0)
])

// ["a", false, 0]
MyTuple(["a"])
```

**tuple**

```ts
const MyTuple = type(["string", ["boolean", "=", false], ["number", "=", 0]])

// ["a", false, 0]
MyTuple(["a"])
```

### optional

An optional element may be absent from the input and has no default.

Optional elements follow the prefix and defaultable elements, and come before a variadic element or the end of the tuple. Like in TypeScript, they can't be combined with postfix elements.

**string**

```ts
const MyTuple = type(["string", "boolean?", "number?"])

// ["a"]
MyTuple(["a"])
```

**fluent**

```ts
const MyTuple = type([
	type.string,
	type.boolean.optional(),
	type.number.optional()
])

// ["a"]
MyTuple(["a"])
```

**tuple**

```ts
const MyTuple = type(["string", ["boolean", "?"], ["number", "?"]])

// ["a"]
MyTuple(["a"])
```

### variadic

Like in TypeScript, a variadic element allows zero or more consecutive values of a type. A tuple can have at most one. Write it as `"..."` followed by an array:

**string**

```ts
// a string followed by zero or more numbers
const MyTuple = type(["string", "...", "number[]"])
```

**fluent**

```ts
// a string followed by zero or more numbers
const MyTuple = type([type.string, "...", type.number.array()])
```

### postfix

Postfix elements are required elements after a variadic element. They can't be combined with optional or defaultable elements.

**string**

```ts
// zero or more numbers followed by a boolean, then a string
const MyTuple = type(["...", "number[]", "boolean", "string"])
```

**fluent**

```ts
// zero or more numbers followed by a boolean, then a string
const MyTuple = type(["...", type.number.array(), type.boolean, type.string])
```

## dates

`Date` allows a valid `Date` instance. An invalid date, like `new Date("x")`, is rejected:

```ts
// ArkErrors: must be a Date (was an invalid Date)
type.Date(new Date("x"))
```

To accept invalid dates everywhere, configure [`dateAllowsInvalid`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#dateallowsinvalid).

### literals

A date literal, `d'...'` or `d"..."`, is a `Date` with an exact value. They're mostly useful as [range](https://arktype.io/docs/objects#dates-ranges) bounds.

```ts
const Literals = type({
	singleQuoted: "d'1970-01-01'",
	doubleQuoted: 'd"1970-01-01"'
})
```

A literal, like a string passed as a date limit, must be the same instant on every machine, so it can be an ISO date like `2025-01-01` (which is UTC), an ISO date-time with `Z` or an offset like `2025-01-01T12:00+01:00`, or a number of epoch milliseconds. Any other literal, like `d'notadate'` or `d'2025-01-01T12:00'`, is a `ParseError`.

### ranges

Constrain a `Date` with `>`, `>=`, `<` or `<=`. A bound is either a [date literal](https://arktype.io/docs/objects#dates-literals) or a number of milliseconds since the Unix epoch.

**string**

```ts
const Bounded = type({
	inThePast: `Date < ${Date.now()}`,
	from2000: "Date >= d'2000-01-01'",
	before2100: "Date < d'2100-01-01'"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Bounded = type({
	inThePast: type.Date.earlierThan(Date.now()),
	from2000: type.Date.atOrAfter("2000-01-01"),
	before2100: type.Date.earlierThan("2100-01-01")
})
```

The fluent methods are `laterThan`, `atOrAfter`, `earlierThan` and `atOrBefore`.

A range sets both bounds at once, each inclusive or exclusive:

**string**

```ts
const tenYearsAgo = new Date().setFullYear(new Date().getFullYear() - 10)

const Recent = type(`${tenYearsAgo} <= Date < ${Date.now()}`)
```

**fluent**

```ts
const tenYearsAgo = new Date().setFullYear(new Date().getFullYear() - 10)

const Recent = type.Date.atOrAfter(tenYearsAgo).earlierThan(Date.now())
```

Descriptions and error messages write dates in UTC. A date at UTC midnight is written as its calendar date, or just its year on January 1:

```ts
// "a Date and 2023 or later"
type("Date >= d'2023-01-01'").description

// "a Date and January 1, 2023, 2:30 PM UTC or later"
type("Date >= d'2023-01-01T14:30Z'").description
```

## instanceof

Most built-in classes like `Array`, `Date` and `Map` are [keywords](https://arktype.io/docs/keywords#instanceof). Use `instanceof` for your own classes:

**fluent**

```ts
class MyClass {}

const Instance = type.instanceOf(MyClass)
```

**tuple**

```ts
class MyClass {}

const Instance = type(["instanceof", MyClass])
```

**args**

```ts
class MyClass {}

const Instance = type("instanceof", MyClass)
```

> **Array is the only constructor that works across realms**
>
> Constructors are compared by identity, so a value created in another realm, like an `<iframe>` or a `node:vm` context, is not an instance of the constructor in yours. `Array` is checked with `Array.isArray`, so it also matches arrays from another realm.

### keywords

The [keywords](https://arktype.io/docs/keywords#instanceof) page lists every built-in class keyword, along with the subtypes of [Array](https://arktype.io/docs/keywords#array) and [FormData](https://arktype.io/docs/keywords#formdata).

Keywords for web platform classes, like `Blob`, `File`, `URL`, `FormData`, `Headers`, `Request` and `Response`, throw when used in a runtime that doesn't define that class, e.g. `'Blob' is unresolvable`.

# Keywords

> Every built-in keyword, from TypeScript's own types to subtypes like string.email and generics like Pick.

## TypeScript

TypeScript's built-in types are keywords, except `any` and `void`, which don't mean anything useful at runtime. If you need `any`, use `unknown.any`.

**string**

```ts
const Keywords = type({
	string: "string",
	date: "Date"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Keywords = type({
	string: type.string,
	date: type.Date
})
```

These keywords are attached directly to `type`: `string`, `number`, `bigint`, `boolean`, `symbol`, `undefined`, `null`, `object`, `unknown`, `true`, `false`, `never`, `Key`, `Array`, `Date`, `Record` and `arrayIndex`. Every keyword is available in `type.keywords`.

## Subtypes

A subtype keyword refines or transforms its parent, like `string.email` or `string.date.parse`. To find them in your editor, start a definition like `"string."` and let autocomplete list them.

**string**

```ts
const Keywords = type({
	dateString: "string.date",
	isoDateString: "string.date.iso",
	parsedDate: "string.date.parse",
	parsedIsoDate: "string.date.iso.parse"
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Keywords = type({
	dateString: type.keywords.string.date.root,
	isoDateString: type.keywords.string.date.iso.root,
	parsedDate: type.keywords.string.date.parse,
	parsedIsoDate: type.keywords.string.date.iso.parse
})
```

A keyword with subtypes, like `string.date`, is a module. Its `.root` is the keyword's own `Type`.

## All keywords

These are all the keywords `type` resolves. To define your own, see [scopes](https://arktype.io/docs/scopes).

### string

| - | - |

### FormData

| Alias | Description |
| - | - |
| `FormData` | a FormData instance |
| `FormData.parse` | a morph from a FormData instance to an object representing parsed form data |
| `FormData.parsed` | an object representing parsed form data |
| `FormData.value` | a string or a File instance |

### TypedArray

| Alias | Description |
| - | - |
| `TypedArray.BigInt64` | a BigInt64Array |
| `TypedArray.BigUint64` | a BigUint64Array |
| `TypedArray.Float32` | a Float32Array |
| `TypedArray.Float64` | a Float64Array |
| `TypedArray.Int16` | an Int16Array |
| `TypedArray.Int32` | an Int32Array |
| `TypedArray.Int8` | an Int8Array |
| `TypedArray.Uint16` | a Uint16Array |
| `TypedArray.Uint32` | a Uint32Array |
| `TypedArray.Uint8` | a Uint8Array |
| `TypedArray.Uint8Clamped` | a Uint8ClampedArray |

### instanceof

| Alias | Description |
| - | - |
| `Blob` | a Blob instance |
| `Date` | a Date |
| `Error` | an Error |
| `File` | a File instance |
| `Function` | a function |
| `Headers` | a Headers instance |
| `Map` | a Map |
| `Promise` | a Promise |
| `RegExp` | a RegExp |
| `Request` | a Request instance |
| `Response` | a Response instance |
| `Set` | a Set |
| `URL` | a URL instance |
| `WeakMap` | a WeakMap |
| `WeakSet` | a WeakSet |

### generic

| Alias | Description |
| - | - |
| `Exclude` | exclude branches of a union like \`Exclude("boolean", "true")\` |
| `Extract` | extract branches of a union like \`Extract("0 \| false \| 1", "number")\` |
| `Merge` | merge an object's properties onto another like \`Merge(User, { isAdmin: "true" })\` |
| `Omit` | omit a set of properties from an object like \`Omit(User, "age")\` |
| `Partial` | make all named properties of an object optional like \`Partial(User)\` |
| `Pick` | pick a set of properties from an object like \`Pick(User, "name \| age")\` |
| `Record` | instantiate an object from an index signature and corresponding value type like \`Record("string", "number")\` |
| `Required` | make all named properties of an object required like \`Required(User)\` |

# Expressions

> Combine, refine, transform and annotate types with operators like unions, intersections, narrows, pipes, brands and metadata.

An expression combines or modifies other definitions. Most expressions can be written four ways:

- **string**: embedded in a string definition, like `"string | number"`
- **fluent**: a method on a `Type`, like `type.string.or(type.number)`
- **tuple**: an array definition, like `["string", "|", "number"]`
- **args**: the same elements passed to `type` as arguments, like `type("string", "|", "number")`

They're interchangeable, so use whichever reads best. Where an operand is a function or a value like a symbol, use the fluent, tuple or args form.

| Expression | String | Fluent | Tuple / args |
| - | - | - | - |
| [intersection](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#intersection) | `"a & b"` | `.and(b)` | `[a, "&", b]` |
| [union](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#union) | `"a \| b"` | `.or(b)` | `[a, "\|", b]` |
| [array](https://arktype.io/docs/objects#arrays) | `"a[]"` | `.array()` | `[a, "[]"]` |
| [keyof](https://arktype.io/docs/objects#properties-keyof) | `"keyof a"` | `.keyof()` | `["keyof", a]` |
| [brand](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#brand) | `"a#name"` | `.brand("name")` | |
| [narrow](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#narrow) | | `.narrow(fn)` | `[a, ":", fn]` |
| [filter](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#filter) | | `.filter(fn)` | |
| [pipe](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#pipe) | | `.pipe(fn)` | `[a, "=>", fn]` |
| [to](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#to) | `"a \|> b"` | `.to(b)` | `[a, "\|>", b]` |
| [unit](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#unit) | a literal, `"'a'"` | `type.unit(value)` | `["===", value]` |
| [meta](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#meta) | | `.configure(meta)` | `[a, "@", meta]` |
| [instanceof](https://arktype.io/docs/objects#instanceof) | | `type.instanceOf(Class)` | `["instanceof", Class]` |

Optional (`?`), defaultable (`=`) and spread (`...`) definitions only apply to properties and tuple elements. They're covered on the [objects](https://arktype.io/docs/objects) page.

## Intersection

Like its TypeScript counterpart, an intersection creates a `Type` that enforces the constraints of both operands.

**string**

```ts
// an email address at arktype.io
const ArkEmail = type("string.email & /@arktype\\.io$/")

// ArkErrors: must be matched by @arktype\.io$ (was "a@b.com")
ArkEmail("a@b.com")
```

**fluent**

```ts
// an email address at arktype.io
const ArkEmail = type("string.email").and(/@arktype\.io$/)

// ArkErrors: must be matched by @arktype\.io$ (was "a@b.com")
ArkEmail("a@b.com")
```

**tuple**

```ts
// an email address at arktype.io
const ArkEmail = type(["string.email", "&", /@arktype\.io$/])

// ArkErrors: must be matched by @arktype\.io$ (was "a@b.com")
ArkEmail("a@b.com")
```

**args**

```ts
// an email address at arktype.io
const ArkEmail = type("string.email", "&", /@arktype\.io$/)

// ArkErrors: must be matched by @arktype\.io$ (was "a@b.com")
ArkEmail("a@b.com")
```

> **To combine properties, merge instead**
>
> Intersecting objects is more work to compute than [merging](https://arktype.io/docs/objects#merge) them, both when the type is created and in your editor. Unless you need overlapping keys' values intersected, merge.

### n-ary

`type.and` intersects any number of definitions:

```ts
// Type<{ foo: string; bar: number; baz: string }>
const FooBarBaz = type.and(
	{ foo: "string" },
	{ bar: "number" },
	{ baz: "string" }
)
```

## Union

A union allows a value that satisfies either operand. ArkType discriminates unions automatically: where a value like its type or a literal key tells the branches apart, it checks that first instead of trying each branch, which keeps validation fast and errors specific.

**string**

```ts
const StringOrNumber = type("string | number")

// ArkErrors: must be a number or a string (was boolean)
StringOrNumber(true)
```

**fluent**

```ts
const StringOrNumber = type.string.or(type.number)

// ArkErrors: must be a number or a string (was boolean)
StringOrNumber(true)
```

**tuple**

```ts
const StringOrNumber = type(["string", "|", "number"])

// ArkErrors: must be a number or a string (was boolean)
StringOrNumber(true)
```

**args**

```ts
const StringOrNumber = type("string", "|", "number")

// ArkErrors: must be a number or a string (was boolean)
StringOrNumber(true)
```

When no branch matches the discriminant, like a value of the wrong type here, the error's code is `discriminant`. See [errors](https://arktype.io/docs/errors) for the fields it carries.

### n-ary

`type.or` unions any number of definitions:

```ts
// Type<string | number | { key: unknown }>
const Union = type.or(type.string, "number", { key: "unknown" })
```

> **A union that could transform the same input in different ways throws a ParseError**
>
> ```ts
> // operands overlap, but neither transforms data
> const Okay = type("number > 0").or("number < 10")
>
> // an operand transforms data, but the inputs don't overlap
> const AlsoOkay = type("string.numeric.parse").or({ box: "string" })
>
> // ParseError: An unordered union of a type including a morph and a type with overlapping input is indeterminate
> const Bad = type({ box: "string.numeric.parse" }).or({ box: "string" })
> ```
>
> **Why this isn't allowed**
>
> `Bad` says two things about the same input:
>
> - if `box` is a string, parse it as a number
> - if `box` is a string, keep it as a string
>
> The order of a union's branches doesn't affect its result, so there's no way to choose between them. The same applies when the transformed keys differ: `type({ a: "string.numeric.parse" }).or({ b: "string.numeric.parse" })` throws too, since an input like `{ a: "1", b: "2" }` matches both branches and each would parse a different key.

### extract / exclude

`.extract()` keeps the branches of a union that are assignable to a definition, and `.exclude()` removes them, like TypeScript's `Extract` and `Exclude`:

```ts
const Primitive = type("string | number | boolean")

// Type<number | boolean>
const NumberOrBoolean = Primitive.extract("number | boolean")

// Type<number | boolean>
const NotString = Primitive.exclude("string")
```

In a definition, use the `Extract` and `Exclude` [generics](https://arktype.io/docs/generics#keywords), e.g. `"Exclude<'a' | 'b' | 0, string>"`.

## Brand

A brand adds a type-only tag to a type, so the only values that satisfy it are those you validated with it.

**string**

```ts
const Even = type("(number % 2)#even")
type Even = typeof Even.infer

const good: Even = Even.assert(2)
// TypeScript: Type 'number' is not assignable to type 'Brand<number, "even">'
const bad: Even = 5
```

**fluent**

```ts
const Even = type.number.divisibleBy(2).brand("even")
type Even = typeof Even.infer

const good: Even = Even.assert(2)
// TypeScript: Type 'number' is not assignable to type 'Brand<number, "even">'
const bad: Even = 5
```

A brand changes nothing at runtime. The `Brand` type it infers is exported from `arktype`.

For more on branding in general, see [this article](https://www.learningtypescript.com/articles/branded-types) by [Josh Goldberg](https://github.com/joshuakgoldberg).

## Narrow

A narrow adds custom validation to a type. Return `true` to accept the value, or call `ctx.mustBe()` or `ctx.reject()` to reject it with a message. The [intro](https://arktype.io/docs/intro/adding-constraints#narrow) walks through an example.

**fluent**

```ts
const Palindrome = type("string").narrow(
	(s, ctx) => s === [...s].reverse().join("") || ctx.mustBe("a palindrome")
)

// ArkErrors: must be a palindrome (was "arktype")
Palindrome("arktype")
```

**tuple**

```ts
const Palindrome = type([
	"string",
	":",
	(s, ctx) => s === [...s].reverse().join("") || ctx.mustBe("a palindrome")
])

// ArkErrors: must be a palindrome (was "arktype")
Palindrome("arktype")
```

**args**

```ts
const Palindrome = type(
	"string",
	":",
	(s, ctx) => s === [...s].reverse().join("") || ctx.mustBe("a palindrome")
)

// ArkErrors: must be a palindrome (was "arktype")
Palindrome("arktype")
```

`ctx.reject()` can also set the error's `path` and `actual`, e.g. to report a mismatch at the right key without printing a password:

```ts
const Form = type({
	password: "string",
	confirmPassword: "string"
}).narrow(
	(data, ctx) =>
		data.password === data.confirmPassword ||
		ctx.reject({
			expected: "identical to password",
			actual: "",
			path: ["confirmPassword"]
		})
)

// ArkErrors: confirmPassword must be identical to password
Form({ password: "arktype", confirmPassword: "artkype" })
```

If a narrow's return type is a type predicate, the `Type` infers it:

```ts
// Type<`ark${string}`>
const ArkString = type("string").narrow(
	(data, ctx): data is `ark${string}` =>
		data.startsWith("ark") || ctx.reject("a string starting with 'ark'")
)
```

The [traversal API](https://arktype.io/docs/traversal-api) documents everything `ctx` can do.

## Filter

`filter` is like `narrow`, but checks a type's **input** instead of its output. The difference matters when the type transforms its input:

- **`narrow`** checks the **output**, after morphs run
- **`filter`** checks the **input**, before morphs run

```ts
const ShortNumeric = type("string.numeric.parse").filter(
	// s is the input string, not the parsed number
	(s, ctx) => s.length <= 10 || ctx.reject("at most 10 characters")
)

// 123
ShortNumeric("123")

// ArkErrors: must be at most 10 characters (was "12345678901")
ShortNumeric("12345678901")
```

Like `narrow`, a type predicate returned by a filter is inferred, here as the type's input.

## Pipe

A pipe transforms data after it is validated, through one or more functions called **morphs**. The [intro](https://arktype.io/docs/intro/morphs-and-more) walks through examples.

**fluent**

```ts
// Type<(In: string) => Out<string>>
const TrimStart = type("string").pipe(str => str.trimStart())
```

**tuple**

```ts
// Type<(In: string) => Out<string>>
const TrimStart = type(["string", "=>", str => str.trimStart()])
```

**args**

```ts
// Type<(In: string) => Out<string>>
const TrimStart = type("string", "=>", str => str.trimStart())
```

A morph receives the validated value itself rather than a copy, so a morph that mutates its argument mutates the caller's data. [By default](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#mutatesinput), ArkType writes to its input only to transform a builtin like a Date, Map or function, which it transforms in place. Any other transformed object is a new object that shares every untransformed value with the input, and input that nothing transforms is returned as is.

```ts
const T = type({ a: "string.trim", b: { c: "string" } })
const input = { a: " x ", b: { c: "y" } }

const out = T.assert(input)

out === input // false
out.b === input.b // true
```

The exception is a builtin object ArkType doesn't copy, like a function, `Promise`, `WeakMap`, `FormData`, `Blob` or boxed primitive, which is transformed in place.

### To

A morph can return `ArkErrors` to fail validation, so a `Type` works as a morph: it validates the previous output. The `to` operator pipes to a definition without wrapping it in `type`:

**string**

```ts
// Type<(In: string) => To<number>>
const ParseEven = type("string.numeric.parse |> number % 2")

// ArkErrors: must be even (was 3)
ParseEven("3")
```

**fluent**

```ts
// Type<(In: string) => To<number>>
const ParseEven = type("string.numeric.parse").to("number % 2")

// ArkErrors: must be even (was 3)
ParseEven("3")
```

**tuple**

```ts
// Type<(In: string) => To<number>>
const ParseEven = type(["string.numeric.parse", "|>", "number % 2"])

// ArkErrors: must be even (was 3)
ParseEven("3")
```

**args**

```ts
// Type<(In: string) => To<number>>
const ParseEven = type("string.numeric.parse", "|>", "number % 2")

// ArkErrors: must be even (was 3)
ParseEven("3")
```

`.to("number % 2")` is the same as `.pipe(type("number % 2"))`.

### n-ary

`.pipe()` accepts any number of morphs and types. `type.pipe()` does the same without a `Type` to start from:

```ts
// Type<(In: string) => To<string>>
const TrimStartNonEmpty = type.pipe(
	type.string,
	s => s.trimStart(),
	type.string.atLeastLength(1)
)

// ArkErrors: must be non-empty
TrimStartNonEmpty("   ")
```

## Unit

A [literal](https://arktype.io/docs/primitives#number-literals) is the simplest way to allow one exact primitive value. To allow a value a string can't embed, like a `symbol`, use `type.unit` or `===`:

**fluent**

```ts
const mySymbol = Symbol()

const ExactValue = type.unit(mySymbol)
```

**tuple**

```ts
const mySymbol = Symbol()

const ExactValue = type(["===", mySymbol])
```

**args**

```ts
const mySymbol = Symbol()

const ExactValue = type("===", mySymbol)
```

## Enumerated

`type.enumerated` allows any of a list of values. With one value, it's the same as `type.unit`.

**fluent**

```ts
const mySymbol = Symbol()

const ExactValueFromSet = type.enumerated(1337, true, mySymbol)
```

**tuple**

```ts
const mySymbol = Symbol()

const ExactValueFromSet = type(["===", 1337, true, mySymbol])
```

**args**

```ts
const mySymbol = Symbol()

const ExactValueFromSet = type("===", 1337, true, mySymbol)
```

## valueOf

`type.valueOf` allows the values of a TypeScript `enum` or an enum-like object:

```ts
enum TsEnum {
	numeric = 1
}

// Type<TsEnum.numeric>
const EnumType = type.valueOf(TsEnum)
```

It is almost the same as `type.enumerated(...Object.values(o))`. The difference is an entry whose key is another entry's numeric value, mapping back to that entry's key. That's how TypeScript compiles a numeric `enum`, so `valueOf` skips the reverse entry:

```ts
// what TsEnum compiles to
const equivalentObject = {
	numeric: 1,
	"1": "numeric"
} as const

// allows only 1, though it infers Type<1 | "numeric">
const EquivalentType = type.valueOf(equivalentObject)
```

> **Prefer enumerated**
>
> TypeScript is moving away from features that emit JavaScript, like `enum`, which [`--erasableSyntaxOnly`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig/#erasableSyntaxOnly) disallows. `type.valueOf` is for code that already uses `enum`. Otherwise, list values with [`type.enumerated`](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#enumerated) or a literal union.

## fn

`type.fn` wraps a function so its parameters, and optionally its return value, are validated when it's called. Parameters use tuple syntax. Put a return type after `":"`.

```ts
const len = type.fn("string | unknown[]", ":", "number")(s => s.length)

len("foo") // 3
len([1, 2]) // 2

// TraversalError: value at [0] must be a string or an object (was boolean)
len(true)
// TypeScript: Argument of type 'boolean' is not assignable to parameter of type 'string | unknown[]'.
```

The result is a `TypedFn`, which is introspectable:

```ts
const len = type.fn("string | unknown[]", ":", "number")(s => s.length)

len.expression // "(string | Array) => number"
len.params.expression // "[string | Array]"
len.returns.expression // "number"
```

Parameters can be defaultable, optional or variadic:

```ts
const greet = type.fn("string = 'world'")(name => `Hello, ${name}!`)

greet() // "Hello, world!"

const join = type.fn("...", "string[]")((...parts) => parts.join(","))

join("a", "b") // "a,b"
```

Without a return type, the return type is inferred from the implementation and not validated.

## Meta

Metadata attaches information to a type. ArkType reads some of it, like `description`, which error messages use. You can read the rest from the type's `meta`.

**fluent**

```ts
const SpecialString = type("string").configure({
	description: "a special string"
})

// .describe() is shorthand for a description
const SpecialNumber = type("number").describe("a special number")

// ArkErrors: must be a special number (was a string)
SpecialNumber("five")
```

**tuple**

```ts
const SpecialString = type([
	"string",
	"@",
	{
		description: "a special string"
	}
])

// a string is shorthand for a description
const SpecialNumber = type(["number", "@", "a special number"])

// ArkErrors: must be a special number (was a string)
SpecialNumber("five")
```

**args**

```ts
const SpecialString = type("string", "@", {
	description: "a special string"
})

// a string is shorthand for a description
const SpecialNumber = type("number", "@", "a special number")

// ArkErrors: must be a special number (was a string)
SpecialNumber("five")
```

A configured description, like any message you configure, takes precedence over the [locale](https://arktype.io/docs/i18n#your-own-messages), so it isn't translated.

The `keyword` key is reserved: built-in keywords set `meta.keyword` to their name so a locale can find their phrase, and configuring a description removes it. Name your own metadata something else.

To configure only some of a type's nodes, pass a selector after the metadata:

**fluent**

```ts
const Point = type({
	x: "number",
	y: "number"
}).configure(
	{ description: "a coordinate" },
	// every domain node: the object and both numbers
	"domain"
)

// ArkErrors: x must be a coordinate (was a string)
Point({ x: "1", y: 2 })
```

**tuple**

```ts
const Point = type([
	{
		x: "number",
		y: "number"
	},
	"@",
	{ description: "a coordinate" },
	// every domain node: the object and both numbers
	"domain"
])

// ArkErrors: x must be a coordinate (was a string)
Point({ x: "1", y: 2 })
```

**args**

```ts
const Point = type(
	{
		x: "number",
		y: "number"
	},
	"@",
	{ description: "a coordinate" },
	// every domain node: the object and both numbers
	"domain"
)

// ArkErrors: x must be a coordinate (was a string)
Point({ x: "1", y: 2 })
```

Selectors are documented with [`select`](https://arktype.io/docs/internals/nodes#select).

## Cast

A cast changes how a `Type` is inferred without changing what it validates:

**string**

```ts
// any string, but the editor suggests "foo" and "bar"
type AutocompletedString = "foo" | "bar" | (string & {})

const MyObj = type({
	autocompletedString: "string" as type.cast<AutocompletedString>
})
```

**fluent**

```ts
// any string, but the editor suggests "foo" and "bar"
type AutocompletedString = "foo" | "bar" | (string & {})

const MyObj = type({
	autocompletedString: type.string.as<AutocompletedString>()
})
```

## Parenthetical

Operators have the same precedence as in TypeScript, and parentheses group them the same way:

```ts
// Type<{ stringOrNumbers: string | number[]; stringsOrNumbers: (string | number)[] }>
const Groups = type({
	stringOrNumbers: "string | number[]",
	stringsOrNumbers: "(string | number)[]"
})
```

## this

`this` references the root of the definition it's in, which makes the type recursive:

```ts
const DisappointingGift = type({
	label: "string",
	"box?": "this"
})

const out = DisappointingGift({
	label: "foo",
	box: { label: "bar", box: {} }
})

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	// ArkErrors: box.box.label must be a string (was missing)
	console.error(out.summary)
} else {
	// narrowed inference to arbitrary depth
	console.log(out.box?.box?.label)
	// (property) label: string | undefined
}
```

In a scope, `this` is a `ParseError`. Reference the alias by name instead, as described in [cyclic types](https://arktype.io/docs/scopes#cyclic-types):

```ts
const types = scope({
	DisappointingGift: {
		label: "string",
		"box?": "DisappointingGift"
	}
}).export()
```

# Match

> Branch on the type of a value with ArkType definitions, like a type-safe switch statement.

`match` pairs ArkType definitions with handlers. It returns a function that runs the handler of the first case its input satisfies.

## Case record API

Each key is a definition and each value is a handler. The handler's parameter is inferred from its key:

```ts
import { match } from "arktype"

const toLabel = match({
	string: s => s,
	number: n => n.toFixed(2),
	bigint: b => `${b}n`,
	default: "assert"
})

toLabel("abc") // "abc"
toLabel(5) // "5.00"
toLabel(5n) // "5n"
// TraversalError: must be a string, a number or a bigint (was boolean)
toLabel(true)
```

Cases are checked in the order they are defined. A matcher is complete once it has a `default`.

## Default

`default` decides what happens to input that matches no case:

| `default` | Accepts | When no case matches |
| - | - | - |
| `"assert"` | `unknown` | throws a `TraversalError` |
| `"never"` | only input the cases accept | throws a `TraversalError` |
| `"reject"` | `unknown` | returns `ArkErrors` |
| a function | `unknown` | returns the function's result |

```ts
import { match } from "arktype"

const sizeOf = match({
	string: s => s.length,
	number: n => n,
	default: "reject"
})

// ArkErrors: must be a string or a number (was boolean)
sizeOf(true)
```

## Fluent API

`.case(definition, handler)` adds one case at a time, which is convenient for definitions that can't be written as a key. It can follow a case record or start a chain as `match.case(...)`. `.default(...)` completes the matcher:

```ts
import { match } from "arktype"

const sizeOf = match({
	string: s => s.length,
	number: n => n
})
	// any object with a numeric length
	.case({ length: "number" }, o => o.length)
	.default(() => 0)

sizeOf("abc") // 3
sizeOf({ name: "David", length: 5 }) // 5
sizeOf(null) // 0
```

## Input with `in`

`.in<T>()` sets the input type of a matcher: calling it with anything else is a type error, and each handler's parameter is narrowed from `T`. It does not validate at runtime.

`.in(definition)` takes a definition instead and validates input against it before any case runs:

```ts
import { match } from "arktype"

const half = match.in("number | string").match({
	number: n => n / 2,
	default: s => s
})

half(4) // 2
// ArkErrors: must be a number or a string (was boolean)
half(true)
// TypeScript: Argument of type 'boolean' is not assignable to parameter of type 'string | number'.
```

## Properties with `at`

`.at(key)` matches cases against the value of one property. Each handler receives the whole object:

```ts
import { match } from "arktype"

type Data = { id: 1; count: number } | { id: 2; label: string }

const describe = match
	.in<Data>()
	.at("id")
	.match({
		1: o => `${o.count} items`,
		2: o => o.label,
		default: "assert"
	})

describe({ id: 1, count: 3 }) // "3 items"
describe({ id: 2, label: "two" }) // "two"
// TraversalError: id must be 1 or 2 (was undefined)
describe({ count: 3 })
// TypeScript: Property 'id' is missing in type '{ count: number; }' but required in type '{ id: 1; count: number; }'.
```

`match.at(key, cases)` does the same in one call.

## Scoped aliases

`match` resolves the same keywords as `type`. To match on your own aliases, use the `match` method of your [scope](https://arktype.io/docs/scopes):

```ts
import { scope } from "arktype"

const $ = scope({ Id: "string", Count: "number" })

const describe = $.match({
	Id: id => `user ${id}`,
	Count: n => `${n} users`,
	default: "assert"
})

describe("42") // "user 42"
```

# Codecs

> Pair a morph with its inverse to encode output back into input.

A Type with morphs decodes input into output. A codec is a morph with an inverse, so its output can also be encoded back into input.

## Defining a codec

`codec` takes an input definition, an output definition and a function for each direction. It comes from `arktype/codecs`, which installs encoding when imported, so an app that doesn't encode doesn't ship it:

```ts
import { codec } from "arktype/codecs"

const EpochMs = codec("number.integer", "Date", {
	decode: n => new Date(n),
	encode: d => d.getTime()
})

// Date
const date = EpochMs(0)
// 0
const ms = EpochMs.encode(date)
```

A codec is a Type. `.encode` is a Type too, from output to input, so it validates what it receives like any other Type:

```ts
// ArkErrors: must be a Date (was string)
const out = EpochMs.encode("0")
```

What `encode` returns is validated against the input definition, so encoding always produces something the codec can decode.

## Composition

Every Type has `.encode`, which inverts each of its morphs, so a codec encodes wherever it is nested: in objects, arrays and tuples, unions, intersections, pipes and cyclic scopes.

```ts
const Event = type({
	name: "string",
	at: EpochMs,
	"reminders?": EpochMs.array()
})

// { name: "launch", at: 0, reminders: [60000] }
const encoded = Event.encode({
	name: "launch",
	at: new Date(0),
	reminders: [new Date(60000)]
})
```

A Type without morphs encodes as itself.

## Defaults and unions

A defaulted key is always present in decoded output, so it is required when encoding:

```ts
const Settings = type({ since: EpochMs.default(0) })

// ArkErrors: since must be a Date (was missing)
const out = Settings.encode({})
```

A union encodes a value with a branch that accepts it, trying the branches without morphs first, so a value a branch would decode unchanged is encoded unchanged.

## Keywords

The parse keywords encode back to the string they parse: `string.date.parse`, `string.date.iso.parse` and `string.date.epoch.parse`, `string.numeric.parse`, `string.integer.parse`, `string.json.parse` and `string.url.parse`.

```ts
const Event = type({
	at: "string.date.iso.parse",
	count: "string.integer.parse"
})

// { at: "1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z", count: "5" }
const encoded = Event.encode({ at: new Date(0), count: 5 })
```

`string.trim`, `string.lower`, `string.upper`, `string.capitalize` and `string.normalize` encode a string already in their format as itself, and `object.json.stringify` encodes by parsing.

## Precompiling

[Precompiled](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile) Types encode too. The build precompiles each `codec` like any other Type, passing its `decode` and `encode` functions where you wrote them, and each `.encode` it sees read becomes an encoder of its own:

```ts
import { codec } from "arktype/codecs"

const EpochMs = codec("number.integer", "Date", {
	decode: n => new Date(n),
	encode: d => d.getTime()
})

export const Event = type({ at: EpochMs })

// precompiled to an encoder
export const encode = (event: unknown) => Event.encode(event)
```

A standalone build installs encoding itself, so `.encode` works there even if the program never imports `arktype/codecs`. A Type with a morph that has no inverse fails the build where its `.encode` is read, since arktype would throw there.

## Morphs without an inverse

Encoding is only possible if every morph has an inverse. Otherwise, accessing `.encode` throws a `ParseError`:

```ts
const Length = type({ length: type("string").pipe(s => s.length) })

// ParseError: A morph must have an inverse to be encoded: (In: string) => Out<unknown>
Length.encode
```

# Scopes

> Define aliases that reference each other, then use them in definitions or export them as a module of Types.

A scope is a set of named definitions, called aliases, that can reference each other the same way they reference keywords like `string`. The `type` function you import from `arktype` is a method of ArkType's default scope.

## Defining a scope

Pass `scope` an object mapping alias names to definitions:

```ts
import { scope } from "arktype"

const $ = scope({
	Id: "string",
	User: { id: "Id", friends: "Id[]" },
	UsersById: { "[Id]": "User" }
})
```

Aliases are autocompleted and validated like built-in keywords. Write definitions inside a scope directly: wrapping one in `type(...)` fails, because `type` only knows built-in keywords (see [thunks](#thunks)).

`$.type` parses a definition that can reference the scope's aliases. Types created this way keep their scope, so chained methods can reference the aliases too:

```ts
const Group = $.type({ name: "string", members: "User[]" })

const OwnedGroup = Group.and({ ownerId: "Id" })
```

`$.match`, `$.declare`, `$.generic` and `$.fn` work like their counterparts on `type`, but also resolve the scope's aliases.

## Modules

`.export()` turns a scope into a `Module`, an object mapping each alias to its `Type`:

```ts
const types = $.export()

// ArkErrors: friends[1] must be a string (was a number)
types.User({ id: "99", friends: ["7", 8, "9"] })
```

To get a single `Type`, use `$.resolve("User")`.

`type.module` defines a scope and exports it in one call:

```ts
const types = type.module({
	Id: "string",
	User: { id: "Id", friends: "Id[]" }
})
```

A `Module` can be spread into another scope to include all of its aliases. Pass names to `.export()` to include only those:

```ts
const numbers = scope({ Three: "3", Sixty: "60", No: "'no'" })

const superScope = scope({
	...$.export(),
	...numbers.export("Three", "Sixty"),
	Saiyan: { powerLevel: "number > 9000" }
})
```

## Cyclic types

Aliases can reference themselves and each other:

```ts
const types = scope({
	Package: {
		name: "string",
		"dependencies?": "Package[]",
		"contributors?": "Contributor[]"
	},
	Contributor: {
		email: "string.email",
		"packages?": "Package[]"
	}
}).export()
```

Cyclic types are inferred to any depth, and they validate cyclic data:

```ts
type Package = typeof types.Package.infer

const packageData: Package = {
	name: "arktype",
	dependencies: [{ name: "typescript" }],
	contributors: [{ email: "david@sharktypeio" }]
}

// arktype now depends on itself
packageData.dependencies![0].dependencies = [packageData]

// ArkErrors: contributors[0].email must be an email address (was "david@sharktypeio")
types.Package(packageData)
```

A cycle must pass through an object, array or morph. An alias that resolves to itself without one, like `a` in `scope({ a: "a | string" })`, is a type error and throws a `ParseError`.

For a single recursive `Type`, you don't need a scope: use the [`this`](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#this) keyword.

> **Cyclic types may display as any**
>
> TypeScript shows an anonymous cycle as `...`, or as `any` if `noErrorTruncation` is enabled. Either way, the type itself is accurate: you get completions, and accessing a property that doesn't exist is an error.

## Visibility

Aliases prefixed with `#` are private. They can be referenced in the scope, but are not exported:

```ts
const shapes = scope({
	"#BaseShape": { perimeter: "number", area: "number" },
	// reference private aliases without the "#"
	Ellipse: { "...": "BaseShape", radii: ["number", "number"] },
	Rectangle: { "...": "BaseShape", width: "number", height: "number" }
})

// shapes.type can still reference private aliases
const PartialShape = shapes.type("Partial<BaseShape>")

const shapeModule = shapes.export()
Object.keys(shapeModule) // ["Ellipse", "Rectangle"]
```

### `import()`

`.import()` is like `.export()`, but makes every alias private. Spread it into a scope to use another scope's aliases without re-exporting them:

```ts
const utilities = scope({
	"WithId<o extends object>": { "...": "o", id: "string" }
})

const userModule = type.module({
	...utilities.import(),
	Payload: { name: "string", age: "number" },
	Db: "WithId<Payload>"
})

Object.keys(userModule) // ["Payload", "Db"]
```

## Submodules

Keywords like `string.email` are grouped into submodules. To group your own aliases, assign a `Module` to an alias and reference its members with a `.`:

```ts
const ids = type.module({ User: "string", Order: "number" })

const $ = scope({
	Id: ids,
	Customer: { id: "Id.User", orderIds: "Id.Order[]" }
})
```

Submodules are parsed bottom-up: the root scope can reference a submodule's aliases, but a submodule can't reference the root scope's aliases.

### Nested

Submodules can be nested to any depth:

```ts
const store = scope({ Store: $.export() })

const OrderIds = store.type("Store.Id.Order[]")
```

### Rooted

A submodule can't be referenced as a `Type` itself unless it has an alias named `root`, the way `string` is both a keyword and the prefix of `string.email`:

```ts
const userModule = type.module({
	root: { name: "string" },
	// subaliases can reference root like any other alias
	Admin: { "...": "root", isAdmin: "true" },
	Saiyan: { "...": "root", powerLevel: "number > 9000" }
})

const types = type.module({
	User: userModule,
	// User refers to the root alias
	Group: "User[]",
	// or prefixes its subaliases
	ElevatedUser: "User.Admin | User.Saiyan"
})
```

## Thunks

A common mistake is wrapping a scoped definition in `type`:

```ts
const $ = scope({
	Id: "string",
	User: type({
		name: "string",
		id: "Id"
		// TypeScript: 'Id' is unresolvable
	})
})
```

`Id` exists in the scope, but `type` only knows built-in keywords. Here the wrapper is redundant, so remove it:

```ts
const $ = scope({
	Id: "string",
	User: {
		name: "string",
		id: "Id"
	}
})
```

To use fluent methods like `.pipe` on a scoped definition, define it as a thunk: a function that calls the `type` method of the scope you're defining.

```ts
const $ = scope({
	Id: "string",
	TrimmedId: () => $.type("Id").pipe(s => s.trim())
})

const types = $.export()

types.TrimmedId("  42 ") // "42"
```

## Configuration

`scope` takes a config as its second argument. It applies to every `Type` parsed in the scope:

```ts
const $ = scope({ Even: "number % 2" }, { divisor: { expected: "even" } })

// ArkErrors: must be even (was 3)
$.export().Even(3)
```

It accepts the same options as [global configuration](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration), except these, which can only be configured globally: `onUndeclaredKey`, `numberAllowsNaN`, `numberAllowsInfinity`, `dateAllowsInvalid`, `keywords` and `locale`.

# Generics

> Declare definitions with parameters and instantiate them like TypeScript generics.

A generic is a definition with parameters. Instantiating it with a definition for each parameter returns a `Type`.

## Keywords

Like TypeScript's utility types, these generics are available in any definition:

| Alias | Description |
| - | - |
| `Exclude` | exclude branches of a union like \`Exclude("boolean", "true")\` |
| `Extract` | extract branches of a union like \`Extract("0 \| false \| 1", "number")\` |
| `Merge` | merge an object's properties onto another like \`Merge(User, { isAdmin: "true" })\` |
| `Omit` | omit a set of properties from an object like \`Omit(User, "age")\` |
| `Partial` | make all named properties of an object optional like \`Partial(User)\` |
| `Pick` | pick a set of properties from an object like \`Pick(User, "name \| age")\` |
| `Record` | instantiate an object from an index signature and corresponding value type like \`Record("string", "number")\` |
| `Required` | make all named properties of an object required like \`Required(User)\` |

Instantiate one in a string, or call it from `type.keywords`:

```ts
const One = type("Extract<0 | 1, 1>")

const Unfalse = type.keywords.Exclude("boolean", "false")
```

`Record` is also available as `type.Record`. Generics like `Pick` and `Partial` have [method equivalents](https://arktype.io/docs/objects#properties-pick-omit) on object Types, such as `User.pick("name")`.

## Syntax

### Definition

Pass a string of parameter names in angle brackets, then a definition that references them:

```ts
const BoxOf = type("<t>", { box: "t" })

// Type<{ box: string }>
const StringBox = BoxOf("string")
```

`type.generic("t")({ box: "t" })` is equivalent.

### Constraints

Constrain a parameter with `extends`. Arguments must satisfy the constraint, and the definition can use the parameter wherever its constraint is allowed, like with the `>` operator here:

```ts
const NonEmpty = type("<arr extends unknown[]>", "arr > 0")

// Type<number[]>
const NonEmptyNumbers = NonEmpty("number[]")

// ParseError: arr must be assignable to Array (was string)
NonEmpty("string")
// TypeScript: ["Invalid argument for arr", expected: unknown[]]
```

With `type.generic`, pass a `[name, constraint]` tuple: `type.generic(["arr", "unknown[]"])("arr > 0")`.

### Scoped

In a [scope](https://arktype.io/docs/scopes), declare parameters in the alias name:

```ts
const types = scope({
	"Box<t, u>": { box: "t | u" },
	BitBox: "Box<0, 1>"
}).export()

// ArkErrors: box must be 0 or 1 (was 2)
types.BitBox({ box: 2 })
```

### Recursive

A scoped generic can reference itself:

```ts
const types = scope({
	"Tree<t>": { value: "t", "children?": "Tree<t>[]" },
	NumberTree: "Tree<number>"
}).export()

// ArkErrors: children[0].value must be a number (was a string)
types.NumberTree({ value: 1, children: [{ value: "2" }] })
```

## HKT

`generic()` with an `Hkt` class wraps a type-level TypeScript function as an ArkType generic. The function transforms the arguments at runtime, and the class's `body` describes the result at the type level. This is how `Partial` is implemented:

```ts
import { generic, Hkt } from "arktype"

const Partial = generic(["T", "object"])(
	args => args.T.partial(),
	class PartialHkt extends Hkt<[object]> {
		declare body: Partial<this[0]>
	}
)

// Type<{ a?: string }>
const PartialA = Partial({ a: "string" })
```

For more examples, see the [generic tests](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/blob/HEAD/ark/type/__tests__/generic.test.ts).

## External

To write a TypeScript function that accepts and returns Types, constrain a parameter with `type.Any`:

```ts
const createBox = <t extends string>(of: type.Any<t>) =>
	type({
		box: of
	})

// @ts-expect-error
createBox(type("number"))

// Type<{ box: string }>
const BoxType = createBox(type("string"))
```

To accept a definition instead, validate it with `type.validate` and infer the result with `type.instantiate`:

```ts
const createBox = <const def>(
	of: type.validate<def>
): type.instantiate<{ box: def }> =>
	type.raw({
		box: of
	}) as never

// Type<{ box: string }>
const BoxType = createBox("string")
```

TypeScript generics like these can be hard to get right. If yours isn't inferring as expected, see [the FAQ](https://arktype.io/docs/faq#why-isnt-my-wrapper-generic-working).

# Declare

> Define a Type that must match an existing TypeScript type exactly.

If your ArkType definitions are your source of truth, infer your TypeScript types from them: `type User = typeof User.infer`.

If the TypeScript type comes first, `type.declare` checks that a definition matches it. Object keys are autocompleted, and a definition that is too wide _or_ too narrow is a type error:

```ts
type Expected = { a: string; b?: number }

const T = type.declare<Expected>().type({
	a: "string",
	"b?": "number"
})

const Bad = type.declare<Expected>().type({
	a: "string",
	// narrower than number
	"b?": "1"
	// TypeScript: declared: number; inferred: 1;
})
```

Optionality can also be expressed in the value instead of the key:

```ts
type Expected = { a: string; b?: number }

const T = type.declare<Expected>().type({
	a: "string",
	// same as "b?": "number"
	b: "number?"
})
```

`declare` works with any definition, not only objects:

```ts
const Name = type.declare<string>().type("string")

const Entry = type.declare<[string, number]>().type(["string", "number"])
```

To reference your own aliases, use the `declare` method of your [scope](https://arktype.io/docs/scopes), like `$.declare<User>().type(...)`.

## `side`

A Type with morphs or defaults has different input and output types. For example, `string.numeric.parse` accepts a `string` and returns a `number`.

By default, `declare` compares your definition to the declared type as a whole, so a morph only matches if the declared type includes it. To compare only the input or output, pass `{ side: "in" }` or `{ side: "out" }`:

```ts
type Expected = { a: number; b?: number }

const Bad = type.declare<Expected>().type({
	a: "string.numeric.parse",
	// TypeScript: declared: number; inferred: (In: string) => To<number>;
	"b?": "number"
})

// the output must match Expected
const T = type.declare<Expected, { side: "out" }>().type({
	a: "string.numeric.parse",
	"b?": "number"
})
```

# Validation

> Check data against a Type by calling it, asserting it or testing it with allows.

## Calling a Type

A Type is a function. Call it with any data and it returns either the validated output or `ArkErrors`:

```ts
const User = type({
	name: "string",
	age: "number.integer >= 0"
})

const out = User({ name: "Alan", age: 41.5 })

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	// age must be an integer (was 41.5)
	console.error(out.summary)
} else {
	// out is { name: string; age: number }
	console.log(out.name)
}
```

`type.errors` is the `ArkErrors` class, so `instanceof` narrows the result. Invalid data never throws unless you configure [`onFail`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#onfail). See [Errors](https://arktype.io/docs/errors) for what `ArkErrors` contains.

The output is the data after [morphs](https://arktype.io/docs/intro/morphs-and-more) and defaults have run, so it can differ from the input:

```ts
const Form = type({ age: "string.numeric.parse" })

// { age: 41 }
Form({ age: "41" })

// ArkErrors: age must be a well-formed numeric string (was "forty")
Form({ age: "forty" })
```

## assert

`.assert` returns the output or throws a [`TraversalError`](https://arktype.io/docs/errors#traversalerror), for when invalid data is a bug rather than something to handle:

```ts
const Form = type({ age: "string.numeric.parse" })

// { age: 41 }
const form = Form.assert({ age: "41" })

// TraversalError: age must be a well-formed numeric string (was "forty")
Form.assert({ age: "forty" })
```

## from

`.from` is `.assert` with its argument typed as the Type's input, so TypeScript checks data you write by hand:

```ts
const User = type({ name: "string", age: "number" })

// { name: "David", age: 34 }
const david = User.from({ name: "David", age: 34 })

// TypeScript: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'
const typo = User.from({ name: "David", age: "34" })
```

## allows

`.allows` returns a boolean and narrows its argument, without building errors or running morphs:

```ts
const User = type({ name: "string", age: "number" })

const data: unknown = { name: "David", age: 34 }

if (User.allows(data)) {
	// data is { name: string; age: number }
	console.log(data.name)
}

const Numeric = type("number | bigint")

// [0, 2n]
const numerics = [0, "one", 2n].filter(Numeric.allows)
```

On a Type with a morph, `.allows` checks only the input, so data can be allowed and still fail when the Type is called:

```ts
const AtLeast6 = type("string.numeric.parse").to("number >= 6")

// true, since "3" is a numeric string
AtLeast6.allows("3")

// ArkErrors: must be at least 6 (was 3)
AtLeast6("3")
```

## Standard Schema

Every Type implements [Standard Schema](https://arktype.io/docs/standard-schema), so libraries that accept one can validate with it through `~standard.validate`. ArkType validates synchronously, and a failure result is the `ArkErrors` itself, whose `issues` is an array of `ArkError`:

```ts
const User = type({ name: "string", age: "number" })

const result = await User["~standard"].validate({ name: "David", age: "34" })

if (result.issues) {
	// age must be a number (was a string)
	console.log(result.issues[0].message)
} else {
	// { name: string; age: number }
	console.log(result.value)
}
```

## Custom checks

To add your own check, use [`.narrow`](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#narrow). To transform data, use [`.pipe`](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#pipe). Both receive a [`ctx`](https://arktype.io/docs/traversal-api) for reporting errors.

# Errors

> Read, serialize and throw the errors a Type returns for invalid data.

## ArkErrors

A Type called with invalid data returns `ArkErrors`, which holds one error for each path that failed:

```ts
import { flatProblemsByPath, type } from "arktype"

const User = type({
	name: "string",
	age: "number >= 0"
})

const out = User({ name: 5, age: -1 })

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	// age must be non-negative (was -1)
	// name must be a string (was a number)
	console.error(out.summary)

	// ["age must be non-negative (was -1)",
	//  "name must be a string (was a number)"]
	out.issues.map(error => error.message)

	// { age: ["must be non-negative (was -1)"],
	//   name: ["must be a string (was a number)"] }
	flatProblemsByPath(out)
}
```

`ArkErrors` isn't an array. Its errors are in `issues`, so index them, iterate them or call array methods there.

| member | what it is |
| - | - |
| `issues` | an array with one error per path, in the order each path first failed |
| `summary`, `toString()` | every error's message, one per line |
| `count` | how many errors were added, more than `issues.length` when several failed at one path |
| `toJSON()` | an array of each error's JSON, with its `propString` |
| `toLocaleString(locale?)` | the summary in a [locale](https://arktype.io/docs/i18n#rendering-in-a-locale) |
| `throw()` | throws a [`TraversalError`](#traversalerror) |

`arktype` exports functions that group an `ArkErrors` by path:

| function | what it returns |
| - | - |
| `byPath(out)` | an object mapping each path's `propString` to its error |
| `flatByPath(out)` | like `byPath`, but each value is an array, with an `intersection` split into its errors |
| `flatProblemsByPath(out)` | like `flatByPath`, but with each error's `problem` |
| `byAncestorPath(out)` | each failed path and its ancestors, with `""` for the root, mapped to every error at or below it |
| `messageIn(error, locale)` | one error's message in a [locale](https://arktype.io/docs/i18n#rendering-in-a-locale) |

A Type that calls no narrow or morph may find its errors' issues only when they're first read, so rejecting data costs little more than the check that rejected it. The issues describe the data as it is at that read: a write to it in between can change them, and data that no longer fails holds one root issue, `is invalid`. A getter or `Proxy` trap the check reads runs again at that read, and what it throws is thrown there. Each error's text is written at that first read too.

## ArkError

Each error in `issues` is a plain object, typed as `ArkError`, describing what failed at one path:

```ts
const out = type({ age: "number >= 0" })({ age: -1 })

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	const error = out.issues[0]

	error.code // "min"
	error.path // ["age"]
	error.propString // "age"
	error.data // -1
	error.expected // "non-negative"
	error.actual // "-1"
	error.problem // "must be non-negative (was -1)"
	error.message // "age must be non-negative (was -1)"

	// narrow by code to read its own fields
	if (error.code === "min") error.rule // 0
}
```

Its message is built from parts: `message` puts the path before `problem`, which reads "must be `expected` (was `actual`)". You can [configure each part](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#error-messages).

An error also has `meta`, the metadata of the Type that failed, and usually a `description`. It has no methods, so `JSON.stringify(error)` serializes its own keys, and `messageIn(error, locale)` writes its message in another locale.

When several checks fail at one path, they are merged into one error with the code `intersection`. `flatByPath` splits it back up:

```ts
import { flatProblemsByPath, type } from "arktype"

const out = type({ n: "number % 2 >= 2" })({ n: 1 })

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	// n (1) must be...
	//   ◦ even
	//   ◦ at least 2
	console.error(out.summary)

	// { n: ["must be even (was 1)", "must be at least 2 (was 1)"] }
	flatProblemsByPath(out)
}
```

## Error codes

An error's `code` tells you its other fields:

| code | fields |
| - | - |
| `domain` | `domain`, like `"string"` |
| `unit` | `unit`, the expected value |
| `proto` | `proto`, the expected constructor |
| `min`, `max` | `rule`, and `exclusive` when the bound is exclusive |
| `minLength`, `maxLength`, `exactLength` | `rule` |
| `divisor` | `rule` |
| `pattern` | `rule` (the regex source) and `flags` |
| `before`, `after` | `rule`, a `Date` |
| `predicate` | `predicate` when a narrow returns `false`; `morph` and what it threw as `cause` for `pipe.try`; `meta.keyword` and sometimes `cause` for a keyword's parse |
| `required` | `missing`, the missing value's type; `valueMeta`, its meta; and `missingValueDescription`, its English description |
| `undeclared` | none; its `data` is the value of a key `"+": "reject"` disallows |
| `discriminant` | `discriminantKind`, `cases`, `onKey` and `absent` |
| `union` | `errors`, one per branch |
| `intersection` | `errors`, one per check that failed at the path |

Each also has `data` and `path`, and `meta` unless `ctx` or `pipe.try` raised it. Built-in keywords with their own text, like `string.email`, set `meta.keyword` to their name.

`discriminant` is a miss of a union ArkType checks by switching on a domain or a literal value: branches with different domains, like `number | null`, three or more literals, like `"a" | "b" | "c"`, or objects with a discriminant key. Its `data` is the discriminant's value, and `cases` lists the values or domains it expected. Other unions, including two literals like `"a" | "b"`, report `union`:

```ts
const Shape = type({ kind: "'circle'", r: "number" }).or({
	kind: "'square'",
	side: "number"
})

const out = Shape({ kind: "triangle" })

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	const error = out.issues[0]

	// kind must be "circle" or "square" (was "triangle")
	error.message

	// ["circle", "square"]
	if (error.code === "discriminant") error.cases
}
```

## TraversalError

`.assert`, `.from` and `ArkErrors`' `throw()` throw a `TraversalError`, which extends `Error`. A single error's message is its summary. Several are listed on their own lines after a leading newline:

```ts
import { flatProblemsByPath, type, TraversalError } from "arktype"

try {
	type({ a: "string", b: "number" }).assert({ a: 1, b: "x" })
} catch (e) {
	if (e instanceof TraversalError) {
		// "\n  • a must be a string (was a number)\n  • b must be a number (was a string)"
		e.message

		// the ArkErrors, for structured access
		flatProblemsByPath(e.arkErrors)
	}
}
```

`arkErrors` is non-enumerable, so loggers that print an error's own properties skip it.

## ParseError

A `ParseError` is thrown when a definition is invalid, as the Type is created rather than when it validates. TypeScript reports the same mistakes in your editor, so you'll usually see one only for definitions TypeScript can't check, like strings built at runtime:

```ts
import { ParseError, type } from "arktype"

const def: string = "string | numbr"

try {
	type.raw(def)
} catch (e) {
	// ParseError: 'numbr' is unresolvable
	if (e instanceof ParseError) console.error(e.message)
}
```

# Traversal API

> The ctx argument that narrow and pipe functions receive for reading the current path and reporting errors.

Functions you pass to [`.narrow`](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#narrow) and [`.pipe`](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#pipe) receive a `ctx` as their second argument. Use it to report errors that read like ArkType's own:

```ts
const Even = type("number").narrow(
	(n, ctx) => n % 2 === 0 || ctx.mustBe("even")
)

// ArkErrors: must be even (was 3)
Even(3)
```

A narrow returns `ctx.mustBe(...)` or `ctx.reject(...)`, which add an error and return `false`. A morph returns `ctx.error(...)`, which adds an error and returns it:

```ts
const Json = type("string").pipe((s, ctx) => {
	try {
		return JSON.parse(s)
	} catch {
		return ctx.error("valid JSON")
	}
})

// ArkErrors: must be valid JSON (was "{")
Json("{")
```

`reject` and `error` take a string or the parts of an error. `relativePath` reports it below the current path:

```ts
const Range = type({ start: "number", end: "number" }).narrow(
	(range, ctx) =>
		range.start <= range.end ||
		ctx.reject({
			expected: "at least start",
			actual: `${range.end}`,
			relativePath: ["end"]
		})
)

// ArkErrors: end must be at least start (was 1)
Range({ start: 2, end: 1 })
```

To write a check outside the call, type `ctx` with `Traversal`:

```ts
import { type, type Traversal } from "arktype"

const isEven = (n: number, ctx: Traversal) => n % 2 === 0 || ctx.mustBe("even")

const Even = type("number").narrow(isEven)
```

## Members

### `path`

the path being validated or morphed

- array indices represented as numbers
- warning: mutated during traversal - use `path.slice(0)` to snapshot
- use [`propString`](#propstring) for a stringified version

### `root`

the original value being traversed

### `config`

configuration for this traversal

- options can affect traversal results and error messages
- defaults < global config < scope config
- does not include options configured on individual types

### `hasError`

whether `currentBranch` (or the traversal root, outside a union) has one or more errors

### `errors`

[ArkErrors](https://arktype.io/docs/errors) that will be part of this traversal's finalized result

- will always be empty for a valid traversal

### `data`

the data being validated or morphed

- the value at [`path`](#path), as transformed by any morphs that have already run

### `propString`

a string representing [`path`](#path)

- uses `.access` [where allowed by JS](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Property_accessors#dot_notation), falling back to `[indexAccess]`

```ts
const path = ["key1", Symbol("key2"), "key3", 4, "~key5"]
const propString = 'key1[Symbol(key2)].key3[4]["~key5"]'
```

### `reject`

add an [ArkError](https://arktype.io/docs/errors) and return `false`

- useful for predicates like `.narrow`

### `mustBe`

add an [ArkError](https://arktype.io/docs/errors) from a description and return `false`

- useful for predicates like `.narrow`
- equivalent to [`reject`](#reject)({ expected })

### `error`

add and return an [ArkError](https://arktype.io/docs/errors)

- useful for morphs like `.pipe`

# Configuration

> Change ArkType's defaults and error messages globally, for a scope or for a single Type.

## Levels

Config can be set at three levels. A more specific level overrides a broader one.

### Global

Call `configure` in its own file, and import that file before anything creates a Type:

```ts
import { configure } from "arktype/config"

configure({ numberAllowsNaN: true })
```

```ts
import "./config.ts"
import { type } from "arktype"

// true
type.number.allows(Number.NaN)
```

> **Configure before any Type is created**
>
> Global config is fixed when the first Type is created, whether by a definition
> or by referencing a keyword like `type.number`, and calling `configure` after
> that throws. Importing `"arktype"` first is fine, and `configure` can be
> imported from either `"arktype"` or `"arktype/config"`.

### Scope

Pass config as the second argument to `scope` or `type.module`. It applies to every Type parsed in that scope:

```ts
const $ = scope(
	{ User: { age: "number < 100" } },
	{ max: { actual: () => "unacceptably large" } }
)

// ArkErrors: age must be less than 100 (was unacceptably large)
$.export().User({ age: 101 })

// ArkErrors: age must be at most 100 (was unacceptably large)
$.type({ age: "number <= 100" })({ age: 101 })
```

### Type

`.configure` adds [metadata](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#meta), like a `description` or [error parts](#error-messages), to a Type. It applies wherever that Type is referenced, but not to the Types inside it:

```ts
// don't print the password
const Password = type("string >= 8").configure({ actual: "" })

const User = type({
	email: "string.email",
	password: Password
})

// ArkErrors: password must be at least length 8
User({ email: "david@arktype.io", password: "ez123" })
```

## Options

| option | default | levels |
| - | - | - |
| [`onUndeclaredKey`](#onundeclaredkey) | `"ignore"` | global, type (`"+"`) |
| [`exactOptionalPropertyTypes`](#exactoptionalpropertytypes) | `true` | global, scope |
| [`numberAllowsNaN`](#numberallowsnan) | `false` | global |
| [`numberAllowsInfinity`](#numberallowsinfinity) | `false` | global |
| [`dateAllowsInvalid`](#dateallowsinvalid) | `false` | global |
| [`jitless`](#jitless) | `false`, or `true` where `new Function` is blocked | global, scope |
| [`onFail`](#onfail) | `null`, which returns `ArkErrors` | global, scope |
| [`errors`](#errors) | `"all"` | global, scope |
| [`mutatesInput`](#mutatesinput) | `false` | global, scope |
| [`keywords`](#keywords) | `{}` | global |
| [`locale`](#locale) | `en` | global |
| [an error code](#by-code), like `divisor` | ArkType's messages | global, scope |
| [`toJsonSchema`](#tojsonschema) | draft 2020-12, throwing for what it can't express | global, scope |

A Type's own options are its [metadata](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#meta), including the [parts of its errors](#error-messages).

## Error messages

Each error message is built from parts. Configure the part you want to change, and ArkType keeps composing the rest, including messages for unions and intersections. `expected`, `actual`, `problem` and `message` each take a string or a function. See [Errors](https://arktype.io/docs/errors) for what an error contains.

### description

What follows "must be" in a message. Other parts and the Type's `.description` reuse it, so it should be your first choice:

```ts
const Even = type("number % 2").describe("an even number")

// ArkErrors: must be an even number (was 3)
Even(3)
```

### expected

Like `description`, but only for error messages, where it takes precedence. A function receives the error, so it can read `code`, `data` and `path`:

```ts
const Password = type("string >= 8").configure({
	expected: ctx =>
		ctx.code === "minLength" ? `${ctx.rule} characters or more` : "a password"
})

// ArkErrors: must be 8 characters or more (was 5)
Password("ez123")

// ArkErrors: must be a password (was a number)
Password(12345678)
```

### actual

What goes inside "(was …)". An empty string omits it. A function receives the data, then the error:

```ts
const Password = type("string >= 8").configure({ actual: "" })

// ArkErrors: must be at least length 8
Password("ez123")
```

### problem

The whole sentence after the path, like "must be a string (was a number)". A function receives the error, including its `expected` and `actual`. It may not apply to the errors of a union:

```ts
const Name = type("string").configure({
	problem: ctx => `${ctx.actual} isn't ${ctx.expected}`
})

// ArkErrors: a number isn't a string
Name(5)
```

### message

The whole message, including the path. A function receives the error, including its `problem`. It may not apply to the errors of a union:

```ts
const User = type({
	password: "string >= 8"
}).configure({
	message: ctx => `${ctx.propString || "(root)"}: ${ctx.problem}`
})

// ArkErrors: (root): must be an object (was a string)
User("ez123")

// .configure applies only at the root, so the nested error is unchanged
// ArkErrors: password must be at least length 8 (was 5)
User({ password: "ez123" })
```

Each function also receives the active [locale](https://arktype.io/docs/i18n#your-own-messages) as its last argument, so it can write its text in the language a message is read in.

### By code
