`number` rejects `Infinity` and `-Infinity`, as it already rejected `NaN`:

```ts
// ArkErrors: must be a number (was Infinity)
// before: Infinity
type.number(Infinity)
```

Allow them everywhere with `configure({ numberAllowsInfinity: true })`, or in one Type with the `number.Infinity` and `number.NegativeInfinity` keywords:

```ts
const T = type("number | number.Infinity | number.NegativeInfinity")
```

### The clone option is removed

Transforming no longer clones the input first. Output shares every value nothing transformed with the input, and a morph receives the validated value itself, so a morph that mutates its argument mutates your data. Remove `clone` from your config.

```ts
const T = type({ a: "string.trim", b: { c: "string" } })
const input = { a: " x ", b: { c: "y" } }

T.assert(input).b === input.b // true, before: false
```

### "+": "delete" removes symbol keys and sorts its output

`"+": "delete"` also removes undeclared symbol keys, and its output has required keys, then optional keys, each sorted, rather than the input's order:

```ts
const T = type({ "+": "delete", b: "string", a: "string" })

T({ b: "2", z: 0, a: "1" }) // { a: "1", b: "2" }, before: { b: "2", a: "1" }
```

### "+": "reject" checks string keys only

`"+": "reject"` allows undeclared symbol keys, so `rejectAllowsSymbolKeys` is gone. Reject types that differ only by a symbol key now overlap, so a union of them with a morph is indeterminate:

```ts
const T = type({ "+": "reject", a: "string" })

// valid, before: ArkErrors: value at [Symbol(s)] must be removed
T({ a: "x", [Symbol("s")]: 1 })
```

### Shallow cycles throw

An alias that resolves to itself without passing through an object, array or morph accepted every value. It now throws a `ParseError`:

```ts
// throws ParseError: Alias 'a' has a shallow resolution cycle: a->a
scope({ a: "a" }).export()
// TypeScript: Alias 'a' has a shallow resolution cycle: a->a
```

## Configuration

### Configure before any Type is created

Global config is fixed when the first Type is created, whether by a definition or by referencing a keyword like `type.number`, and `configure` throws after that, where it used to apply to scopes created later but not to `type` or keywords. Call it in a file of its own, and import that file before anything creates a Type:

```ts
import { configure } from "arktype/config"

configure({ onUndeclaredKey: "delete" })
```

```ts
import "./config.ts"
import { type } from "arktype"
```

### meta.keyword is reserved

Built-in keywords set `meta.keyword` to their name. Rename your own meta named `keyword`.

## Output

These change what `toJsonSchema()`, `.expression` and `.json` return, which matters if you store or snapshot them.

- A union of literals with configured meta becomes `enum`: `type("'a' | 'b'").configure({ title: "Letter" }).toJsonSchema()` is `{ enum: ["a", "b"], title: "Letter" }` instead of an `anyOf` of `const`s.

- A string index signature beside declared keys becomes `patternProperties: { "": ... }` instead of `additionalProperties`.

- `toJsonSchema()` throws for a regex flag JSON Schema can't express, instead of leaving it out: `type(/^a/i).toJsonSchema()` throws (code `patternFlags`), before: `{ type: "string", pattern: "^a" }`, which rejects `"A"`.

- `toJsonSchema()` throws for an index signature key it can't express, instead of leaving out the index signature: `type({ "[string <= 3]": "number" }).toJsonSchema()` throws (code `indexKey`), before: `{ type: "object" }`. See [JSON Schema](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#how-types-map) for the keys it can write.

- Expressions keep length bounds and protos beside a structure: `type("number[] > 1").expression` is `number[] >= 2`, before: `number[]`.

- Optional keys are listed by name, whether or not they have a default: `{ bar?: number, foo: string = "foo" }`, before: `{ foo: string = "foo", bar?: number }`.

- The `$ark.x` names that functions get in `.json` and `.expression` are names only and no longer resolve through `$ark`.

- Keys are ordered by code unit, where they were ordered as `JSON.stringify` writes them, which moves only keys that first differ at a character JSON escapes or where one ends: `"a"` now precedes `"a b"`.

## Inference

- `.required()` makes a defaulted key required in `inferIn`, as it already did at runtime: `type({ foo: "string = 'bar'" }).required()` infers `{ foo: string }` as input, before: `{ foo?: string }`.
- A morph that returns `any` infers `any` as its output: `type({ a: ["string", "=>", s => JSON.parse(s)] }).infer` is `{ a: any }`, before: `{ a: (In: string) => Out<any> }`.

## @ark/schema

- `BaseNode.compiledMeta` is removed, and `BaseScope.resolutions` holds an unresolved alias's parse context instead of its id.

## ArkRegex

A capture in one alternation branch is `undefined` in every other branch, so the inferred tuples line up with what `exec` returns:

```ts
const R = regex("^(?:(1)|(2))$")

// before: ["1"] | [undefined, "2"]
type Captures = typeof R.inferCaptures // ["1", undefined] | [undefined, "2"]
```

## Attest

Runtime benches run in a loop compiled for each bench, after a warmup, so their times don't compare with earlier versions'. Re-record stored runtime baselines.

- A bench should return the result it computes, so V8 can't drop the work. attest warns when a bench returns `undefined`.
- `until.count` and `until.ms` bound the samples taken after the warmup. Before, they counted sets of 1000 calls and time from the bench's start.
- Instantiation counts include evaluating the type a bench returns as fully as displaying it would. Re-record type benches whose results weren't already fully evaluated.

# FAQ

> Answers to common questions about ArkType's behavior, configuration and TypeScript integration.

## Why do I see type errors in an ArkType package in `node_modules`?

This can occur due to incompatibilities between your `tsconfig.json` and ours. It is harmless as long as your types are correct in source.

We recommend enabling [`skipLibCheck`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig/#skipLibCheck) in every TypeScript project to avoid false positives like this and improve editor performance.

## Why does `number` reject `Infinity`?

`number` excludes `NaN`, `Infinity` and `-Infinity` by default, so validated numbers are finite. JSON can't represent them either: `JSON.stringify(Infinity)` is `"null"`. To allow them in one type, add the corresponding keyword:

```ts
const Bound = type("number | number.Infinity | number.NegativeInfinity")
```

To allow them everywhere, configure `numberAllowsInfinity` or `numberAllowsNaN` (see [Configuration](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration)).

## Why can't I index `ArkErrors` like an array?

`ArkErrors` isn't an `Array`. Its errors are in `issues`, one per path:

```ts
const out = type({ name: "string" })({})

if (out instanceof type.errors) {
	// ArkError: name must be a string (was missing)
	out.issues[0]
	out.issues.map(e => e.message)
	for (const error of out.issues) console.log(error.path)
}
```

See [Errors](https://arktype.io/docs/errors) for everything an error carries.

## Why isn't my configuration applied?

Global config is fixed when the first Type is created, by a definition or by reading a keyword like `type.number`. Calling `configure` after that throws a `ParseError`: `configure() must be called before any Type is created`. Put it in its own file and import that file before anything creates a Type. See [Configuration](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration).

## Does a morph change my input?

Only if you mutate it. A morph receives the validated value itself, not a copy, so mutating its argument mutates the caller's data. Return a new value instead:

```ts
const addTag = type({ tags: "string[]" }).pipe(o => ({
	...o,
	tags: [...o.tags, "new"]
}))
```

## Should I precompile?

If your app is bundled, yes. A [precompiled](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile) build ships each Type as a standalone validator, without arktype's parser and without generating code at runtime, and your definitions don't change. Stay dynamic where there's no build step or a program composes Types at runtime. See [Dynamic vs Precompiled](https://arktype.io/docs/dynamic-vs-precompiled).

## Can I get error messages in another language?

Yes. ArkType ships English and German, and you can write a locale for any other language. See [i18n](https://arktype.io/docs/i18n).

## How does ArkType compare to Zod or Valibot?

All three validate at runtime and infer TypeScript types. The main difference is how you write a definition: ArkType uses TypeScript's own syntax, while Zod and Valibot use function calls.

```ts
// z.object({ name: z.string(), age: z.number().int().min(0).optional() })
const User = type({
	name: "string",
	"age?": "number.integer >= 0"
})
```

That means dynamic ArkType parses your definitions at runtime, so it ships a parser, and its bundle is larger than Zod's or Valibot's. [Precompiled](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile), it ships no parser. On Valibot's own login form, precompiled ArkType reports every error, with its message, in a smaller bundle than Valibot: 0.91 kB gzipped against 1.48 kB.

Coming from Zod, most APIs have a direct equivalent:

| Zod | ArkType |
| - | - |
| `z.object({ ... })` | `type({ ... })` |
| `.optional()` on a property | `"key?": ...` |
| `.default(value)` | `"number = 0"` as a property value |
| `z.enum(["a", "b"])` | `"'a' \| 'b'"` |
| `z.array(T)` | `T.array()` or `"string[]"` |
| `z.infer<typeof T>` | `typeof T.infer` |
| `T.parse(data)` | `T.assert(data)` |
| `T.safeParse(data)` | `T(data)`, then `instanceof type.errors` |
| `.refine(fn)` | `.narrow(fn)` |
| `.transform(fn)` | `.pipe(fn)` |

All three implement [Standard Schema](https://arktype.io/docs/standard-schema), so a library that accepts one of them accepts the others.

## Why isn't my wrapper generic working?

TypeScript's generic inference has many edge cases. General patterns for wrapping Types and definitions are outlined [in the Generics docs](https://arktype.io/docs/generics#external).

> **Type-level logic needs a cast**
>
> When implementing a function with a generic return type, you will almost always need to cast in your implementation, either explicitly via `as` or by using an overload.
>
> Think of it as trading internal safety for external precision. As long as the function you're writing will be called many times externally, the overhead is justified. If not, it may not need to be generic at all. A broad return type like `string` as opposed to `${prefix}.${key}` may be sufficient.
>
> **See an example**
>
> ```ts
> // via explicit cast
> const createBox = <const def>(
> 	of: type.validate<def>
> ): type.instantiate<{ box: def }> =>
> 	type.raw({
> 		box: of
> 		// when implementing generics, never is your go-to
> 		// for allowing an arbitrary assignment with less risk than `any`
> 	}) as never
>
> // via overloads
> // only the external signatures are considered on invocation
> function createBox2<const def>(
> 	of: type.validate<def>
> ): type.instantiate<{ box: def }>
> // the signature associated with the implementation is much looser and should
> // be thought of as equivalent to casting in terms of type safety
> function createBox2(of: unknown) {
> 	return type.raw({
> 		box: of
> 	})
> }
>
> // Type<{ box: string }>
> const Box = createBox("string")
> ```
>
> In both cases, we've explicitly annotated the return type we want and used some method of casting internally to allow our implementation. This is a common pattern for implementing generic functions and, more generally, associating an implementation with typings TS can't infer on its own.

For anything more complex, you'll have to rely on your understanding of type manipulation. Tracing your way through ArkType's internal types may uncover helpful patterns, and you may find friendly folks [in our Discord](https://arktype.io/discord) willing to lend a hand.

We can't guarantee your generics will behave the way you expect, since that depends on how TypeScript infers them in your code rather than on ArkType's API.

## What's up with your type/Type casing?

You might have noticed in our documentation we use PascalCase for some Types and camelCase for others:

```ts
const User = type({
	name: "string",
	platform: "'android' | 'ios'",
	"version?": "number | string"
})

const parseJson = type("string.json.parse").to({
	name: "string",
	version: "string.semver"
})
```

Types that only validate are named like TypeScript types. Types that transform their input behave like functions, so they're named like functions.

This distinction evolved from the rules we use for casing our internal TypeScript types:

- Use `PascalCase` for...
  - Entities/non-generic types (e.g. `User`, `SomeData`)
  - Generic types with noun names, like `Array<t>`. As a rule of thumb, your generic should be named this way if all its parameters have defaults (unfortunately TS's built-in `Array` type doesn't have a default parameter, but it probably should have been `unknown`!)

- Use `camelCase` for...
  - Generic types with verb names like `inferDomain<t>`. Types named this way should generally have at least one required parameter.
  - Parameter names, e.g. `t` in `Array<t>`

If you don't like this, feel free to use whatever casing rules best suit your repo. It doesn't affect your Types or scope aliases.

## Is there a way to create an async morph?

Other than handling it as a promise on the output object, no.

As it stands, it doesn't seem worth the significant complexity it would add to morphs in the type system.

If you have a compelling use case, let us know on [this GitHub issue](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/issues/462).
